questions.title: One Trigger Per Object: Handler Framework Design
questions.prompt: A codebase has grown to three or four separate Apex triggers on the same object, each written by a different developer with no shared structure. Explain the 'one trigger per object' pattern, why it matters at enterprise scale, and sketch the shape of a bulkified trigger handler framework that would replace this.
questions.modelAnswer: With multiple triggers on one object, Salesforce does not guarantee their relative execution order, so behavior becomes dependent on metadata creation order and is effectively undefined and unmaintainable once more than one developer touches the object. The 'one trigger per object' pattern collapses all trigger logic for an object into a single trigger that delegates immediately to a handler class, so order of execution within that object is explicit and controlled by the handler rather than by the platform's undocumented trigger-firing order. A proper handler framework implements a common interface or abstract base class with one method per context (beforeInsert, beforeUpdate, afterInsert, afterUpdate, beforeDelete, afterDelete, afterUndelete), a static or instance recursion guard to prevent re-entrant execution when the handler's own DML causes the trigger to fire again, and a bypass mechanism so data migration or test setup code can disable specific handlers without disabling validation entirely. Business logic itself should not live in the handler; the handler should delegate to a domain class (in an fflib-style layered architecture) so the trigger-specific plumbing stays separate from logic that might also need to run from a Platform Event subscriber or an invocable action. This pattern matters most at enterprise scale because governor limits are enforced per-transaction, not per-trigger, so three uncoordinated triggers each doing their own SOQL inside a loop will blow the 100-SOQL-call limit long before a single bulkified handler would.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by explaining the actual risk: when you've got three or four triggers on the same object, nobody — including Salesforce — can tell you for certain which one runs first, and that uncertainty is exactly the kind of bug that only shows up in production under load. So step one is always collapsing everything into a single trigger per object that just calls a handler. I'd sketch the handler as implementing one method per context — beforeUpdate, afterInsert, and so on — with a recursion guard built in from day one, because the moment your afterUpdate does a DML that touches the same object, you need a clean way to stop it looping. And I'm careful to keep the handler itself thin — it delegates to a domain class, because I want that validation logic reusable from a Queueable or a Platform Event handler later, not locked inside trigger context. The governor-limit angle is the one that actually convinces skeptical teams: all those SOQL calls across three separate triggers share the same 100-query ceiling in one transaction, so consolidating isn't just cleaner, it's what keeps a bulk data load from failing outright.
commonMistakes: Assumes Salesforce guarantees execution order across multiple triggers on the same object
Puts business logic directly in the handler instead of delegating to a domain/service class
Forgets a recursion guard, causing infinite or runaway re-entrant execution
No bypass mechanism for data migration or test context, forcing validation rules to be manually disabled
Treats consolidation as a style preference rather than a governor-limit and maintainability necessity
keyPoints: Explains that multi-trigger execution order on one object is undefined/unreliable
Collapses logic into a single trigger per object delegating to a handler
Handler implements one method per trigger context with a recursion guard
Business logic delegated to a domain/service layer, not left in the handler
Ties the pattern to governor-limit risk, not just code style

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why multiple triggers on one object is risky and unmaintainable
Designs a correct bulkified handler framework shape
Separates trigger plumbing from reusable business logic
Connects the pattern to governor-limit consequences at scale

questions.title: Selector, Domain, and Service Layers in an fflib-Style Architecture
questions.prompt: Explain the separation of concerns between selector classes, domain classes, and service classes in an enterprise Apex architecture (the fflib / Apex Enterprise Patterns style), and describe a concrete scenario where skipping this layering causes a real maintenance problem.
questions.modelAnswer: Selector classes own all SOQL for a given object — they are the single place a query against Account, for example, is written, which means field-level security enforcement, standard field sets, and query shape live in one reusable place instead of being copy-pasted across the codebase. Domain classes wrap a list of records of one sObject type and own the validation and business rules that apply to that object regardless of entry point — the same domain method can be called from a trigger handler, an invocable Apex action, or a batch job, so the rule is enforced consistently everywhere instead of once per caller. Service classes are the orchestration layer: they coordinate multiple domains and selectors to accomplish a unit of work that spans objects, such as 'close an opportunity and update the related account's lifetime value,' and they are what UI, API, and scheduled entry points actually call. Skipping this layering most often shows up as duplicated validation: a 'cannot close an opportunity with open approval items' rule gets written inline in the trigger, then a developer building a bulk-close screen writes the same rule again slightly differently in a controller, and the two versions drift until a bulk operation ships a record state that was supposed to be impossible. The layering's real payoff is that a change to the rule, or to the query that backs it, happens in exactly one file, and every caller picks it up automatically.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of it as: selectors answer 'how do I get the data,' domains answer 'is this data valid and what are its own rules,' and services answer 'what multi-object thing am I actually trying to accomplish.' The concrete failure mode I've actually seen is a validation rule like 'you can't close an opportunity with open approvals' getting written once in a trigger and then written again, slightly differently, in a Lightning controller for a bulk-close screen someone built six months later — and of course the two versions disagree, so a bulk action slips through with data the business thought was impossible. If that rule had lived in an OpportunitiesDomain class, both the trigger and the bulk-close controller would call the same method and there'd be nowhere for the drift to happen. So when I'm reviewing new Apex, the first thing I check is whether a SOQL query shows up more than once anywhere outside a selector class — that's usually the tell that the layering got skipped under deadline pressure.
commonMistakes: Writes SOQL directly in triggers/controllers instead of centralizing in selectors
Duplicates validation logic across trigger and UI entry points instead of a shared domain method
Conflates service-layer orchestration with domain-layer single-object rules
Can't give a concrete real-world failure scenario, only an abstract definition
keyPoints: Selectors centralize SOQL and field-security enforcement per object
Domains own single-object business rules callable from any entry point
Services orchestrate multi-object units of work and are what UI/API callers invoke
Gives a realistic duplicated-validation failure scenario from skipping the layering

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes selector, domain, and service responsibilities
Gives a concrete, realistic maintenance failure from skipping the layering
Explains the reuse benefit across multiple entry points

questions.title: Platform Events vs. Change Data Capture vs. Generic Streaming API
questions.prompt: A team needs to notify an external system whenever an Opportunity record changes. One engineer suggests Change Data Capture, another suggests a custom Platform Event, and a third suggests the generic Streaming API with PushTopics. Explain the real differences and when each is the right choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Change Data Capture (CDC) publishes change events automatically whenever a tracked object's records are created, updated, deleted, or undeleted, with a payload that mirrors the changed fields and includes header metadata about the change type — it requires no Apex to publish, just enabling the object in Setup, which makes it the right default when the requirement is genuinely 'tell me whenever this record changes' with no custom business logic about what counts as notable. A custom Platform Event is the right choice when the notification represents a business event rather than a raw data change — for example 'Opportunity moved to Closed Won and exceeded $50k,' which needs Apex logic to decide when to publish and what custom payload shape to send, decoupling the event's meaning from the underlying object's schema. Generic Streaming API with PushTopics is effectively legacy at this point: it requires a SOQL query to define the channel, has tighter event delivery limits, lacks the replay durability of the Enterprise Messaging Platform that backs CDC and Platform Events, and Salesforce's own guidance steers new integrations toward CDC or Platform Events instead. For an Opportunity-change notification specifically, the deciding question is whether the external system needs every field-level change (CDC) or only needs to know about a specific business condition (Platform Event) — if it's the latter, a custom Platform Event published from a domain-layer trigger handler keeps the business logic in Salesforce and keeps the external contract from changing every time someone adds a field to Opportunity.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the team through what each one is actually built for. CDC is the 'just tell me when this record changes, I don't need to write any Apex' option — you flip it on for the object and you get every change, including which fields changed. A custom Platform Event is what you reach for when it's not really a data-change notification, it's a business event — 'this opportunity just became closed-won and crossed fifty grand' — because that needs logic to decide whether to fire, and a payload shape that isn't just a mirror of the Opportunity schema. PushTopics I'd just rule out up front — it's the oldest of the three, it's got worse limits, and Salesforce has been pointing people away from it for years. For this specific case, I'd ask the team one question: does the external system need to know about every field edit, or does it only care about a specific condition? If it's the latter, I'm going with the custom event, because it also means I'm not breaking their integration contract every time someone adds an unrelated field to Opportunity down the road.
commonMistakes: Treats PushTopics as a viable modern option rather than effectively legacy
Doesn't distinguish 'raw data change' (CDC) from 'business event' (custom Platform Event)
Misses that CDC requires no Apex while custom events require publish logic
Doesn't consider that a custom event payload decouples the external contract from schema changes
keyPoints: CDC auto-publishes field-level changes with no Apex required
Custom Platform Events are for business-meaningful conditions requiring publish logic
PushTopics/generic Streaming API is effectively legacy and should be avoided for new work
Decouples external integration contract from underlying schema via custom event payloads

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains CDC's automatic, schema-mirroring behavior
Correctly explains when a custom Platform Event is the better fit
Correctly identifies PushTopics as legacy and why
Gives a clear decision rule for the Opportunity scenario

questions.title: Named Credentials and External Credentials: Why the Split Matters
questions.prompt: Salesforce split the old single Named Credential object into a Named Credential plus a separate External Credential. Explain why this split exists, what each piece owns, and why it's a meaningfully better architecture than hardcoding an endpoint and auth token in Apex.
questions.modelAnswer: In the current model, the External Credential owns the authentication protocol and its parameters — OAuth 2.0 flow type, client ID/secret references, JWT settings, or a custom header scheme — while the Named Credential owns the callout endpoint URL and points to an External Credential for how to authenticate, and a Permission Set or Permission Set Group grants specific users or the running context access to specific authentication parameter sets. This split exists because the old single-object model conflated 'where do I call' with 'how do I authenticate,' which made it impossible to reuse one authentication configuration across multiple endpoints, or to scope different users to different credential sets against the same external system without duplicating the whole configuration. Architecturally, this is a large improvement over hardcoding a token in a Custom Setting or Apex constant because the token itself is never visible to Apex code or exposed in debug logs — the callout framework injects the Authorization header at the HTTP layer after the Apex code has already specified the Named Credential as the callout's base URL — so a credential leak via a logged exception or a code review of a sandbox copy is structurally impossible. It also means credential rotation is an admin operation in Setup, not a deployment: if the external system rotates a client secret, an admin updates the External Credential's principal, and every Apex class that calls out through that Named Credential immediately uses the new secret with zero code change or redeploy.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I explain the split is: the External Credential is the 'how do I log in' and the Named Credential is the 'where am I calling and which login do I use.' Before this split, those were jammed into one object, which meant you couldn't reuse an OAuth config across two different endpoints, or give two different groups of users two different credential sets against the same API, without basically duplicating everything. The real win over hardcoding a token, though, is that Apex never sees the actual secret — the platform injects the auth header for you at the HTTP layer, so there's no path for that token to end up in a debug log or get copied into a sandbox by accident. And when the vendor rotates their client secret, that's an admin updating one record in Setup, not me doing an emergency deploy — which is exactly the kind of operational simplicity I want to point to when someone asks why we didn't just stick a token in a Custom Setting and call it done.
commonMistakes: Conflates Named Credential and External Credential responsibilities
Doesn't explain why credential rotation becomes an admin task instead of a deploy
Misses that the callout framework injects auth headers so Apex never sees the raw secret
Treats this purely as a Setup UI change rather than a real security architecture improvement
keyPoints: External Credential owns authentication protocol/parameters; Named Credential owns endpoint + auth reference
Permission Sets scope which principals/parameter sets a user or context can use
Apex never sees the raw secret; it's injected at the HTTP callout layer
Credential rotation becomes an admin Setup change, not a code deploy

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the division of responsibility between the two objects
Explains the security benefit of Apex never seeing the raw secret
Explains the operational benefit (rotation without a deploy)
Contrasts clearly against hardcoding credentials

questions.title: Salesforce DX Source-Driven Development and 2GP Unlocked Packages
questions.prompt: Explain what 'source-driven development' means in Salesforce DX, how second-generation (2GP) unlocked packages differ from both managed packages and plain change-set-based org development, and why a growing architecture team would adopt this model.
questions.modelAnswer: Source-driven development treats the version-controlled repository, not any single org, as the source of truth for metadata — developers work in disposable scratch orgs created from a project definition file, push and pull changes against git, and every org state is reproducible from source rather than being an opaque accumulation of change sets applied over years. Second-generation unlocked packages are self-contained, versioned units of metadata with explicit dependencies, installed into an org like any package, but — unlike managed packages — their components are fully visible and editable by the installing org's admins, there's no namespace lock-in forcing all future work through the package owner, and components can be removed cleanly via package uninstall because the package tracks exactly what it introduced. This differs from managed packages, which are the right model for an ISV distributing a product to orgs it doesn't control and needs to protect IP in, and from plain change-set-based development, which has no dependency graph, no clean rollback, and makes it nearly impossible to know which metadata belongs to which initiative once multiple teams have been shipping into the same org for years. A growing architecture team adopts unlocked packages specifically to get modularity without vendor lock-in: features can be organized into packages aligned to domains (e.g., a 'Billing' package, a 'Service Console' package), each with its own versioned dependency chain, so a team can build, test, and promote one domain's changes independently while CI validates the package against a fresh scratch org rather than an increasingly stateful sandbox.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mental shift I try to get teams to make is: the org is disposable, the repo is real. In source-driven dev, you spin up a scratch org from your project's definition file, make your change, push it to the repo, and if that scratch org got into a weird state you just delete it and spin up another one — nothing important lived there. Unlocked packages are the piece that makes this scale past one team: unlike a managed package, nothing's hidden from the installing org, there's no namespace tax locking you into one vendor's release cadence, and you can actually uninstall one cleanly because it tracks exactly what it added. Compare that to change-set development, where after a few years nobody can tell you with confidence which custom fields belong to which old project — that's the state I'm usually walking into when a client asks me to help them 'modernize.' So when a team's growing, I push for unlocked packages organized by domain — a Billing package, a Service package — each versioned with its own dependencies, so CI can validate one domain's change against a clean scratch org instead of testing against a sandbox that's been accumulating cruft for five years.
commonMistakes: Confuses unlocked packages with managed packages' visibility/namespace restrictions
Treats change sets as equivalent to source-driven dev just because both deploy metadata
Doesn't mention scratch orgs being disposable/reproducible from source
No concrete reason tied to team growth/domain modularity for adopting packages
keyPoints: Source-driven dev makes the repo, not the org, the source of truth
Scratch orgs are disposable and reproducible from a project definition file
2GP unlocked packages are fully visible/editable and cleanly uninstallable, unlike managed packages
Explains the real-world change-set failure mode (unknown metadata ownership over time)
Ties package modularity to independent team/domain velocity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains source-driven development and scratch org disposability
Correctly distinguishes unlocked packages from managed packages
Correctly distinguishes packages from change-set development
Gives a real organizational reason for adopting the model

questions.title: Bulkification and the SOQL-in-a-Loop Anti-Pattern
questions.prompt: Explain exactly why putting a SOQL query or DML statement inside a for-loop over trigger-context records fails at scale, and show the bulkified rewrite.
questions.modelAnswer: A trigger always executes against a batch of records — up to 200 in a standard DML operation, more for certain data-load paths — so any SOQL or DML statement placed inside a loop over Trigger.new executes once per record in that batch rather than once per transaction. Governor limits (100 SOQL queries and 150 DML statements per transaction in the synchronous context) are enforced per transaction, not per line of code, so a loop-bound query that works fine with a 5-record test in the UI throws System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries the moment a data load or API bulk operation pushes 200 records through the same trigger. The fix is always the same shape: collect the set of related IDs needed across the entire batch first, issue exactly one SOQL query using a WHERE ... IN clause (or a relationship query) to fetch everything needed in one call, build an in-memory map keyed by Id, then iterate the trigger records a second time doing only in-memory lookups and field assignments, and finally issue exactly one DML statement against the collected list or map of records to update. This pattern generalizes beyond triggers to any Apex that processes a collection — Queueable, Batch, and invocable methods are all equally subject to the same governor limits and need the same two-pass collect-then-process shape.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it with the actual failure mode, because that's what makes it stick: a trigger doesn't run once per record, it runs once per batch, and a loop-bound SOQL call means you're issuing one query for every record in that batch. That's invisible in the UI where you're testing with one or two records, and it blows up the second a real data load pushes 200 records through — you get a 'too many SOQL queries' exception that never shows up in dev. The fix I always reach for is the same two-pass shape: first loop just to collect the IDs you need, one query with an IN clause to get everything at once into a map, then a second loop that only does in-memory map lookups and field math, and one DML call at the end. And I make a point of telling junior devs this isn't just a trigger rule — it applies the exact same way inside a Queueable or a Batch Apex execute method, because the governor limits don't care what kind of Apex context you're in.
commonMistakes: Tests only with 1-2 records and never catches the loop-bound query/DML
Doesn't recognize the limit is per-transaction, not per-line or per-record
Writes the collect-IDs step but still issues the DML inside the second loop
Thinks bulkification is trigger-specific rather than applying to Batch/Queueable too
keyPoints: Triggers execute against a batch, so loop-bound SOQL/DML multiplies per record
Governor limits are enforced per transaction, invisible in small-scale UI testing
Correct pattern: collect IDs, one bulk query into a map, second loop for logic, one bulk DML
Same pattern applies to Batch Apex and Queueable, not just triggers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why batch-context loops multiply SOQL/DML calls
Correctly produces the bulkified two-pass rewrite
Explains why small-scale testing hides the bug
Generalizes the pattern beyond triggers

questions.title: Skinny Tables, the Division Field, and Other LDV Query Techniques
questions.prompt: An org has a 40-million-row custom object and report performance is degrading. Explain what a skinny table is, what the Division field does, and how each helps with large data volumes — and the real limitation of each.
questions.modelAnswer: A skinny table is a Salesforce-managed, denormalized copy of a subset of an object's frequently-queried, non-null fields (up to roughly 100 columns), kept in sync automatically with the base table, that avoids the join overhead of the standard data + field-value table structure for reads; it meaningfully speeds up full table scans and reporting against a handful of commonly-filtered fields but must be requested through Salesforce Support or an Account Executive, it excludes certain field types (encrypted fields, long text, multi-select picklists, and formula fields referencing other objects), and it's rebuilt behind the scenes any time its underlying schema changes, which can introduce latency around deployments. The Division field is a legacy multi-tenant partitioning mechanism, available for orgs with Divisions enabled, that lets queries and reports implicitly scope to the user's current working division, effectively reducing the number of rows the query planner has to consider when a Division filter is present or implied — but it's an older feature most orgs never enable, it requires every relevant object to carry and be queried by Division consistently, and it doesn't help at all for queries that legitimately need to span divisions. Neither of these is a substitute for selective SOQL (filtering on an indexed field with reasonably high cardinality) or appropriate custom indexing on the actual object; they're complements that help once the underlying query pattern is already selective. For a 40-million-row object specifically, the first diagnostic step is checking whether reports and SOQL are filtering on indexed, selective fields at all — if they're not, a skinny table request without fixing the query pattern will show far less improvement than expected.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always start with the caveat: neither of these fixes a bad query, they make a good query faster. A skinny table is basically Salesforce keeping a flattened, denormalized copy of your most commonly-queried columns so reads skip the join overhead of the standard schema — it genuinely helps, but you have to request it through Support, it can't include things like encrypted fields or multi-select picklists, and any schema change on those columns triggers a rebuild you need to plan around. The Division field is older and a lot more niche — it's a built-in partition key that narrows what the query planner even has to look at when a division filter applies, but almost nobody has Divisions turned on anymore, and it's useless the moment a query legitimately needs to span multiple divisions. Before I'd request either one for a 40-million-row object, I'd actually go look at the SOQL and the report filters first — if nobody's filtering on an indexed, selective field, a skinny table is going to disappoint everyone, because you can't denormalize your way out of a genuinely non-selective query.
commonMistakes: Treats skinny tables or Division as a substitute for query selectivity, not a complement
Doesn't know skinny tables must be requested through Support, not self-service enabled
Doesn't know which field types are excluded from skinny tables
Recommends Division without checking whether the org even uses Divisions
keyPoints: Skinny table: denormalized, Salesforce-managed subset of fields, avoids join overhead, must be requested
Names real skinny-table exclusions (encrypted, long text, multi-select picklist, cross-object formulas)
Division field: legacy partition key, only helps division-scoped queries
Diagnoses query selectivity as the real first step before requesting either feature

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains skinny tables and their real limitations
Correctly explains the Division field and its narrow applicability
Identifies query selectivity as the real prerequisite diagnostic
Avoids treating either feature as a silver bullet

questions.title: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED vs. WITH USER_MODE in SOQL
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between adding WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED to a SOQL query and running a query in user mode with WITH USER_MODE, and when each enforces what, with a working example of each.
questions.code:
-- WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED: throws at query time if the running user
-- lacks field/object access on any referenced field, including in subqueries
SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue
FROM Account
WHERE Industry = 'Technology'
WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED

-- WITH USER_MODE: enforces FLS, object permissions, AND sharing rules
-- for the running user, filtering rather than throwing
SELECT Id, Name, AnnualRevenue
FROM Account
WHERE Industry = 'Technology'
WITH USER_MODE
questions.modelAnswer: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks field-level security and object permissions for the running user at the moment the query executes, and if the user lacks access to any field or object referenced anywhere in the query (including in a semi-join or subquery), it throws a runtime exception rather than silently filtering — this makes it good for catching an FLS violation loudly during development, but a thrown exception on an otherwise legitimate query is often not the UX a production flow actually wants. WITH USER_MODE, the newer and more complete mechanism, enforces field-level security and object permissions the same way, but additionally enforces sharing rules for the running context, and rather than throwing, it executes the query as that user genuinely would experience it, which is the behavior most SOQL run from a Lightning Web Component or Apex-exposed-to-UI actually needs, since 'this record exists but you can't see it' should usually mean 'it's just not in the result set,' not an unhandled exception. Critically, neither of these replaces explicit sharing enforcement on DML — WITH USER_MODE affects queries; for DML, Apex needs 'as user' Database methods or the stripInaccessible() utility to get equivalent enforcement on writes. The practical rule for an architecture review: any SOQL backing a user-facing component should run WITH USER_MODE (or in a class declared 'with sharing' using as-user DML) rather than WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED by default, because USER_MODE's filter-don't-throw behavior plus sharing enforcement is the closer match to what end users should actually experience.
questions.professionalAnswer: The short version I give people: SECURITY_ENFORCED checks field and object permissions and throws if you're missing access anywhere in the query — including inside a subquery, which trips people up. USER_MODE does everything SECURITY_ENFORCED does, plus it actually enforces sharing rules, and instead of throwing an exception it just filters the results down to what the user can legitimately see — which, for anything backing an LWC or a user-facing flow, is almost always the behavior you actually want. I tell teams: if your SOQL is behind something a user clicks, default to USER_MODE, because 'this record silently isn't in your result set' is a much better user experience than an unhandled exception bubbling up to a Lightning error toast. And I always flag that this only covers reads — for DML, you still need 'as user' database operations or stripInaccessible, because USER_MODE on a query doesn't give you equivalent protection when you go to write.
commonMistakes: Doesn't know USER_MODE additionally enforces sharing rules, unlike SECURITY_ENFORCED
Doesn't know SECURITY_ENFORCED throws while USER_MODE filters silently
Assumes either clause protects DML as well as queries
Doesn't give a concrete recommendation for which to default to in user-facing code
keyPoints: SECURITY_ENFORCED: FLS/object permission check, throws on violation, queries only
USER_MODE: FLS + object permissions + sharing rules, filters rather than throws
Neither replaces DML-side enforcement (as-user DML / stripInaccessible)
Recommends USER_MODE as the default for user-facing query paths

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains SECURITY_ENFORCED's throw-on-violation behavior
Correctly explains USER_MODE's filtering behavior plus sharing enforcement
Correctly notes neither covers DML enforcement
Gives a clear recommendation for user-facing code

questions.title: CRM Analytics: Dataflow vs. Recipe vs. Direct Data Sync
questions.prompt: CRM Analytics (formerly Tableau CRM / Einstein Analytics) offers dataflows, recipes, and direct data connections as ways to get data into a dataset. Explain the real differences and when an architect should choose each.
questions.modelAnswer: A dataflow is the original, JSON-defined ETL pipeline in CRM Analytics, built from discrete nodes (digest, augment, compute expression, sfdcRegister) chained together — it's the most powerful and flexible option, supports complex multi-step transformations and custom Python-like expression logic, but it's also the hardest to maintain and debug because it's authored largely as configuration rather than a visual, inspectable pipeline. A recipe is the modern, visual, drag-and-drop replacement for most dataflow use cases — built in Data Prep with a step-by-step transformation UI (join, filter, bucket, formula) that a business analyst can read and modify without deep technical training, and recipes compile down to run on the same underlying engine, so for net-new work there's rarely a reason to hand-author a dataflow instead of a recipe anymore. Direct data (Live Dataset / Data Sync connections to Salesforce or external sources) skips the transform step and either queries data live at dashboard render time or does a lighter-touch scheduled sync, which is the right choice when the data needs to be closer to real-time and doesn't require heavy reshaping, but it trades away the transformation power of a recipe or dataflow and can hit performance limits against very large or complex live queries. The architectural decision rule: default to recipes for anything requiring real transformation logic because of maintainability, reach for a dataflow only when a specific transformation genuinely can't be expressed in a recipe (a shrinking set of cases as recipes mature), and use direct/live data only for low-latency, lightly-transformed requirements where the freshness requirement outweighs the loss of transformation power.
questions.professionalAnswer: I tell people: dataflow is the original, powerful-but-painful option — it's JSON under the hood, it does almost anything, but debugging it means reading node configuration, not a visual pipeline. Recipes are the thing almost everyone should use now — same underlying engine, but built as a step-by-step visual flow an analyst can actually read and tweak without an engineer, so for any new build I default there. Live or direct data skips transformation almost entirely and either queries Salesforce live or does a light sync — great when the business genuinely needs near-real-time numbers and isn't asking for heavy reshaping, but it'll fall over if someone tries to run a complex live query against a huge dataset. So my actual decision rule is boring: recipe by default, dataflow only for the handful of transforms recipes genuinely still can't express, and live data only when freshness matters more than transformation power.
commonMistakes: Recommends hand-authoring a new dataflow when a recipe would cover the same need
Doesn't know recipes and dataflows run on the same underlying execution engine
Treats live/direct data as always faster, ignoring its performance limits on complex queries
No clear decision rule, just describes the three options without recommending
keyPoints: Dataflow: JSON-defined, powerful, hardest to maintain/debug
Recipe: visual, modern default, same underlying engine as dataflow
Direct/live data: low transformation, best for near-real-time low-complexity needs
Gives a clear default-to-recipe decision rule

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains dataflows and their maintenance tradeoff
Correctly explains recipes as the modern default
Correctly explains direct/live data tradeoffs
Gives a concrete, defensible decision rule

questions.title: Deferred Sharing Calculation and Why Sharing Recalc Is Expensive
questions.prompt: Explain why a role hierarchy or sharing rule change can take hours to process in a large org, what 'deferred sharing calculation' is, and when an architect should proactively request it from Salesforce.
questions.modelAnswer: Sharing recalculation re-evaluates every affected record's access grants across the entire role hierarchy, sharing rules, and territory assignments whenever something structural changes — a user's role, a sharing rule's criteria, a public group's membership — and because this is effectively an all-rows operation on potentially tens of millions of records, the cost scales with both record count and the complexity of the org's sharing model (number of roles, number of sharing rules, group membership depth), not just with how many records actually changed access. Deferred sharing calculation is a feature an architect requests through Salesforce Support that batches up multiple structural changes (role moves, sharing rule edits, group membership changes) during a maintenance window and defers the expensive recalculation until the batch is complete and explicitly resumed, rather than triggering a full recalc after every single change — this is essential during a reorg, a role hierarchy restructuring, or a large group of users changing roles in bulk, where without deferral the system would otherwise recalculate sharing from scratch after every single user move. The sign that an architect should request deferred sharing proactively, rather than reactively, is any planned bulk change to the role hierarchy or a widely-scoped sharing rule in an org with a large enough object (generally LDV territory) that even one full recalculation measurably impacts other users' performance — waiting until a migration already takes six hours to investigate deferred sharing means the org has already paid most of the cost. The broader architectural lesson is that sharing model complexity is itself a performance variable: a flatter role hierarchy with fewer, broader sharing rules recalculates faster than a deep hierarchy with many narrow criteria-based sharing rules, so simplifying the sharing model is sometimes the more durable fix compared to just deferring recalculation around a complex one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as: any structural change to the sharing model — a role move, a sharing rule edit, a group membership change — triggers Salesforce to recompute who can see what, across the whole hierarchy, for every record that could possibly be affected. On a genuinely large object, that's not a quick operation, and the cost isn't really about how many records changed hands, it's about the complexity of the sharing model itself — how many roles, how many rules, how deep the groups go. Deferred sharing calculation is the tool for this: before a planned reorg or a bulk role change, I request it from Support so all those structural changes get batched during a maintenance window instead of triggering a full recalc after every single move. The real tell that you need this proactively, not reactively, is knowing in advance you're about to do a bulk role or group change on a large object — if you're only looking this up after a migration's already eaten six hours of recalc time, you've already paid most of the cost you were trying to avoid. And honestly, sometimes the better long-term fix isn't deferring around a complicated sharing model, it's simplifying the model itself — fewer roles, broader rules, recalculates faster every time, not just during this one migration.

Doesn't know deferred sharing calculation must be requested through Salesforce Support
Requests deferral reactively after a migration is already slow instead of proactively
Doesn't consider simplifying the sharing model itself as a durable alternative fix

Deferred sharing calculation batches structural changes during a maintenance window
Must be requested proactively from Salesforce Support before a planned bulk change
Simplifying the sharing model itself can be a more durable fix than repeatedly deferring recalc

questions.title: Enterprise Territory Management vs. Account Teams for Sales Sharing
questions.prompt: A global sales organization needs account access to follow a complex, multi-dimensional structure (by region, product line, and named key accounts). Compare Enterprise Territory Management against Account Teams as the mechanism for granting that access, and explain when each is the right tool.
questions.modelAnswer: Enterprise Territory Management (the current territory model, successor to the original Territory Management) models access as a hierarchy of territories defined by rule-based or manual account assignment, where a territory can represent a region, a product line, or any combination the business defines, and users are assigned to territories rather than to individual accounts — this scales well because adding a new rep to a territory automatically grants them access to every account the territory's rules already resolve to, and because territory assignment rules can be bulk-recalculated when account attributes change, which keeps access current without manual maintenance. Account Teams, by contrast, grant access at the level of an individual account by adding specific named users with specific team roles (e.g., Sales Rep, Executive Sponsor) directly onto that one account record, which is the right tool for ad hoc, relationship-specific access that doesn't follow a generalizable rule — a named key account where three specific people across different functions need visibility regardless of territory structure. The architectural mistake is trying to force one mechanism to do the other's job: using Account Teams to replicate territory-like bulk access (manually adding the same five people to hundreds of accounts one at a time, with no rule-based recalculation) or using territory rules to express a one-off relationship exception that doesn't generalize to any other account. For the scenario described — region, product line, and named key accounts together — the correct design uses Enterprise Territory Management's hierarchy for the region/product-line dimensions (since those are rule-expressible and apply broadly) and layers Account Teams only on the specific named key accounts that need exception-level, person-specific access beyond what territory membership already grants.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate these by what kind of access they're actually good at. Territory Management is for access that follows a rule — region, product line, whatever dimension — because you assign people to the territory, not the account, and when the territory's rules re-run, access updates itself. Account Teams are for the one-off case: a specific named account where three particular people, maybe across different departments, need visibility that doesn't generalize to any other account. The mistake I see most is people trying to make one do the other's job — manually adding the same five reps to two hundred accounts one at a time because 'territory setup feels complicated,' when that's exactly what territories are for, or conversely trying to force a genuinely one-off relationship exception into a territory rule that doesn't actually generalize. For this org specifically, I'd build the region-and-product-line access as territories, since that's clean rule-based assignment, and then only reach for Account Teams on the handful of truly named key accounts where someone needs exception-level access the territory structure wasn't designed to express.
commonMistakes: Uses Account Teams to manually replicate rule-based bulk access instead of territories
Uses territory rules to express a one-off relationship exception that doesn't generalize
Doesn't know territory assignment rules can be bulk recalculated as account attributes change
Treats the two mechanisms as interchangeable rather than complementary
keyPoints: Territory Management: rule-based, scales to broad dimensions like region/product line
Account Teams: named, person-specific access on individual accounts
Recognizes the anti-pattern of forcing one mechanism to do the other's job
Designs a combined solution using both mechanisms for their appropriate dimension

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Enterprise Territory Management's rule-based scaling model
Correctly explains Account Teams' named, account-level access model

Proposes a correct combined design for the given scenario

questions.title: When a Modern Data Stack Belongs Alongside Salesforce
questions.prompt: A data leadership team asks whether they should stand up Snowflake with dbt and Airflow 'to support Salesforce,' or whether CRM Analytics inside Salesforce is sufficient. Explain the real tradeoffs and when the external modern data stack is architecturally justified.
questions.modelAnswer: CRM Analytics is architecturally right-sized when the analytics requirement is fundamentally Salesforce-centric — dashboards and recipes built mostly from Salesforce objects, consumed mostly by Salesforce users, with transformation needs recipes can express — because it avoids standing up and governing an entirely separate platform, and it keeps the semantic layer close to the CRM data model admins already understand. A modern data stack (Snowflake as the warehouse, dbt for transformation, Airflow for orchestration) becomes justified when any of several conditions hold: the business needs to join Salesforce data against other systems of record (ERP, product usage telemetry, marketing platforms) at a scale or complexity recipes can't express; the organization needs one governed set of metrics definitions shared across Salesforce, a data warehouse, and non-Salesforce BI tools, which argues for a dbt-governed semantic layer rather than definitions duplicated inside CRM Analytics and again inside the warehouse; or the data volume and retention requirements exceed what's economical to keep inside Salesforce's own storage model, in which case Salesforce becomes a source feeding the warehouse (via CDC, Bulk API, or a tool like Fivetran) rather than the analytics engine itself. The two are not mutually exclusive in most mature architectures: Salesforce data flows into Snowflake for cross-system analytics and governed metrics, and operationally relevant subsets flow back into Salesforce (reverse ETL) or into CRM Analytics for the sales/service-rep-facing dashboards that need to live where reps already work. The architectural mistake is framing this as an either/or — the real design question is which analytics consumers need which data, at what latency, in which tool, not whether one platform should replace the other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back gently on the framing — it's usually not 'instead of,' it's 'in addition to, for a different audience.' CRM Analytics is the right call when the analytics are genuinely Salesforce-centric: mostly Salesforce objects, mostly Salesforce users, nothing a recipe can't express. The modern data stack becomes worth the operational overhead when you need to join Salesforce against systems Salesforce doesn't own — ERP, product telemetry, marketing data — or when you need one governed metric definition that both Salesforce and non-Salesforce BI tools read from, instead of someone defining 'active customer' in CRM Analytics and someone else defining it slightly differently in the warehouse. In most mature setups I've seen, both exist together: Salesforce feeds Snowflake for the cross-system, governed analytics, and then either CRM Analytics or a reverse-ETL sync brings the operationally relevant pieces back to where the reps actually work. So my answer to the leadership team is: don't frame it as a replacement decision, frame it as 'which audience, which latency, which tool' — that's the real design question.
commonMistakes: Frames the decision as either/or rather than complementary, audience-specific tools
Doesn't mention governed metric definitions as a key reason to centralize in dbt/warehouse
Ignores reverse ETL as the path for warehouse insights to return to Salesforce users
Recommends the modern data stack without naming a concrete triggering condition
keyPoints: CRM Analytics is right-sized for Salesforce-centric, recipe-expressible analytics
Modern data stack justified for cross-system joins, governed metrics, or scale beyond Salesforce storage
Describes the two coexisting via CDC/Bulk ingestion and reverse ETL
Reframes the question as audience/latency/tool fit rather than a replacement decision

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly characterizes when CRM Analytics alone is sufficient
Names concrete, valid triggers for justifying a modern data stack
Describes how the two coexist (ingestion + reverse ETL)
Reframes the decision correctly rather than as either/or

questions.title: Build a Bulkified Trigger Handler Implementing a Shared Interface
questions.prompt: Implement a trigger handler for a custom object 'Invoice__c' that enforces a validation rule (cannot update Status__c to 'Paid' if Amount_Outstanding__c is greater than zero) in the correct trigger context, using a reusable handler interface pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: The implementation puts the validation entirely inside the before-update context rather than after-update, because addError() on the record is only meaningful before the DML commits — calling it in an after context would require a separate re-query and either a second DML or a different error-surfacing mechanism, both strictly worse. It compares each record's new Status__c against Trigger.oldMap's prior value to detect the specific transition into 'Paid' rather than just checking the current value, because a record that was already 'Paid' with no outstanding balance and is being updated for an unrelated field shouldn't be re-validated or blocked for a condition that was already true before this transaction. The handler takes generic SObject lists and casts internally, which lets it implement a shared ITriggerHandler interface usable by a generic dispatcher across multiple objects, rather than hand-rolling a one-off handler shape per object. This is already bulk-safe as written because it loops once over the batch doing only in-memory comparisons with no SOQL or DML inside the loop, so it scales correctly to a 200-record bulk update without any further changes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put this in before-update, not after, because addError only does something useful before the record's actually been written — if I tried this in an after-save context I'd need a totally different, clunkier way to block the transaction. The other detail I'd call out in review is comparing against the old value, not just checking 'is Status Paid right now' — because otherwise I'd be re-validating records that were already Paid long before this update, for a field that's unrelated to this transition at all. I like using a shared interface here too, even for one object, because it means this handler can plug into a generic dispatcher later without a rewrite — and since there's no SOQL or DML inside the loop, this already works correctly on a 200-record bulk update with zero changes, which is exactly the bar I hold any trigger logic to before I'll approve it.
commonMistakes: Puts the validation in after-update where addError can't block the commit the same way
Checks only the new value instead of comparing against Trigger.oldMap to detect the transition
Introduces a SOQL query inside the loop to look up related data instead of bulk-fetching first
Hand-rolls a one-off handler shape instead of implementing a reusable shared interface
keyPoints: Validation correctly placed in before-update so addError blocks the commit
Detects the specific state transition via Trigger.oldMap, not just the current value
Implements a reusable, generic handler interface rather than a one-off shape
Already bulk-safe: single loop, no SOQL/DML inside it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly places validation in before-update using addError
Correctly detects the transition via old vs. new comparison
Produces genuinely bulk-safe code with no loop-bound SOQL/DML
Uses a reusable interface pattern appropriately

questions.title: Queueable Apex Chaining with a Governor-Limit-Safe Retry
questions.prompt: Write a Queueable Apex class that processes a batch of record IDs via callout, and chains itself to process the next batch, while respecting the queueable depth limit and handling a callout failure with a bounded retry.
questions.modelAnswer: The implementation processes one bounded batch per execute() call rather than the entire list, because a single Queueable execution is still subject to the per-transaction governor limits (including callout limits and CPU time), so a list of thousands of IDs has to be chunked and chained rather than looped through in one invocation. It resets the retry count to zero when chaining to the next batch but increments it only on a retry of the same batch, which correctly distinguishes 'this batch failed and needs another attempt' from 'this batch succeeded, move to the next one' — collapsing those two counters would either retry forever or give up on batches that never actually failed. The bounded retry (MAX_RETRIES) exists because Queueable chaining has no platform-enforced depth limit in the way Batch Apex has a job count limit, but an unbounded retry-on-failure loop against a genuinely down external system would otherwise queue jobs indefinitely and never surface the failure; logging via ErrorLogger after the retry ceiling is what actually surfaces the problem to a human. The check for !Test.isRunningTest() before chaining the next job is necessary because Apex test context only allows one job to be enqueued per test method's Test.startTest/stopTest block, so a real chain would break unit tests that otherwise correctly exercise execute() once.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I always build in deliberately is the chunking — one execute() call only ever handles one bounded batch, because I'm still subject to the same per-transaction limits inside a Queueable as anywhere else, so I can't just loop through a huge ID list in a single run. I keep retry count and 'which batch' logically separate too — resetting it to zero when I successfully move to the next batch, but incrementing it only when the same batch fails — because conflating those either retries forever or silently drops batches that never actually failed. I always cap the retries, because Queueable chaining doesn't have a built-in depth limit the way Batch Apex does, and without a ceiling, a genuinely down external system turns into an infinite queue of retry jobs that never surfaces as an actual problem anyone sees — hence the explicit log call once we give up. And the Test.isRunningTest() check is just a practical necessity: test context only lets you enqueue one job per test, so without that guard this exact chaining pattern breaks every unit test that touches it.
commonMistakes: Processes the entire ID list in one execute() call instead of chunking into bounded batches
Conflates batch-success chaining with retry-count incrementing, causing infinite retries or silent drops
No retry ceiling, risking an effectively infinite chain against a persistently failing callout
Omits the Test.isRunningTest() guard, breaking unit tests that enqueue only one job per test
keyPoints: Chunks work into bounded batches per execute() call to respect per-transaction limits
Correctly separates 'move to next batch' from 'retry this batch' counters
Caps retries with explicit failure logging once the ceiling is hit
Guards chaining behind Test.isRunningTest() for correct unit testability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly chunks and chains batches respecting governor limits
Correctly implements a bounded retry with failure logging
Correctly separates retry logic from batch-progression logic
Handles test context correctly for chained jobs

questions.title: Batch Apex with Database.Stateful for an LDV Reparenting Job
questions.prompt: Write a Batch Apex class that reparents millions of Case records from a deprecated Account to its replacement, tracks a running count of records processed across batches, and uses a selective, indexed query.
questions.modelAnswer: Database.Stateful is required specifically because instance member variables are normally reset between batch chunks — without it, totalProcessed would reset to zero at the start of every execute() invocation instead of accumulating across the entire job, which would make the finish() method's final count meaningless for a multi-million-row object processed across many chunks. The start() method's query filters on AccountId, a standard indexed lookup field, which keeps the query selective even at LDV scale rather than scanning the full Case table; using Database.getQueryLocator rather than an Iterable lets the batch job handle up to 50 million records instead of the much lower limit on a plain Iterable-returning start() method. Database.update(scope, false) with allOrNothing set to false is deliberate: a true value would roll back the entire chunk of up to 200 records if even one record failed validation, silently losing legitimate reparenting for the other 199, whereas partial success lets the job continue and the SaveResult array lets execute() tally exactly how many records in that chunk actually succeeded rather than assuming the whole chunk did. The finish() method's admin notification matters operationally for a bulk job like this because nobody is watching a Batch Apex job interactively the way they'd watch a synchronous operation, so the completion signal and final count need to be pushed out rather than left to be checked manually in Setup.
questions.professionalAnswer: The Database.Stateful piece is the one people forget, and it's the one that matters most here — without it, that running counter resets to zero every single chunk, so by the time finish() runs you'd have no real total, just whatever the last chunk happened to process. I kept the query filtering on AccountId specifically because that's a standard indexed field, so even against a huge Case table this stays selective instead of turning into a full scan — and I used a QueryLocator rather than an Iterable because that's what lets this scale past the much smaller row ceiling an Iterable-based start() is capped at. The allOrNothing=false on the update is deliberate too — I don't want one bad record in a 200-row chunk rolling back the other 199 legitimate reparentings, so I check the SaveResult array and only count what actually succeeded. And I always wire up a completion notification in finish(), because nobody's sitting there watching a batch job's status page — if I don't push a signal out, the only way anyone finds out this ran is by noticing the data looks different.
commonMistakes: Omits Database.Stateful, causing the running total to reset every chunk
Uses Database.update(scope) with default allOrNothing=true, rolling back entire chunks on one bad record
Queries on a non-indexed or non-selective field, causing a full table scan at LDV scale
No completion signal in finish(), leaving a long-running job's result undiscoverable
keyPoints: Database.Stateful correctly used to accumulate a running total across chunks
Query filters on an indexed, selective field appropriate for LDV scale
Partial-success DML with allOrNothing=false, tallying actual successes via SaveResult
finish() pushes a completion notification rather than relying on manual status checks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly uses Database.Stateful for cross-chunk accumulation
Correctly handles partial success with SaveResult tallying
Uses a selective, indexed query appropriate for LDV
Implements a meaningful finish() completion signal

questions.title: Selector Class Enforcing Field-Level Security
questions.prompt: Write a selector class for the Contact object that enforces field-level security on the returned fields using stripInaccessible, and explain why this differs from simply adding WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED to the query.
questions.modelAnswer: This selector combines WITH USER_MODE (which enforces field-level security, object permissions, and sharing on the query itself, filtering rows the user can't see and throwing if the query structure references something entirely inaccessible) with Security.stripInaccessible as a second, explicit pass that strips individual field values the running user lacks read access to from records that are otherwise returned. The reason both matter here is subtle but real: a field the user can't read doesn't necessarily make the whole Contact record inaccessible, so a record can legitimately come back from a USER_MODE query with some of its fields the user shouldn't see still populated in certain edge cases (for instance, fields referenced only in the SELECT list rather than the WHERE clause, or sharing/FLS interactions that differ between row-level and field-level enforcement) — stripInaccessible is the belt-and-suspenders field-level sanitation pass that guarantees the object actually returned to the caller never carries a field value the user can't read, regardless of query-level enforcement nuances. This differs from relying solely on WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED because that clause throws an exception the instant the running user lacks access to any referenced field anywhere in the query, which is unusable for a shared selector called by many different user profiles with varying field access — a reporting-only user hitting this selector would get a hard failure instead of simply receiving records with the fields they can't see omitted. Using Security.stripInaccessible also returns an SObjectAccessDecision object whose getRemovedFields() can be logged or surfaced, giving the architecture visibility into exactly which fields got stripped for which callers, which neither SECURITY_ENFORCED nor USER_MODE alone exposes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I layer two things here on purpose. USER_MODE on the query handles field security, object permissions, and sharing for the running user at the row level. Then stripInaccessible is a second, explicit pass that strips any field values the user shouldn't see off the records that do come back — because the two mechanisms don't always perfectly line up on every field in every edge case, and I want field-level sanitation to be guaranteed, not just implied by the query clause. The reason I didn't just rely on SECURITY_ENFORCED instead is that it throws the second anyone without full field access runs this query — and a shared selector gets called by all kinds of profiles with different field access, so I don't want a reporting user to get a hard exception; I want them to just get records with the fields they can't see quietly omitted. The other thing I like about stripInaccessible specifically is that it hands back an SObjectAccessDecision with the removed fields listed — so if I ever need to debug 'why isn't this field showing up for this user,' I've actually got something to log instead of guessing.
commonMistakes: Relies solely on WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED, causing hard failures for users with partial field access
Skips stripInaccessible entirely, assuming query-level enforcement alone guarantees field sanitation
Doesn't understand SObjectAccessDecision can expose which fields were actually stripped
Puts FLS enforcement logic in the caller instead of centralizing it in the selector
keyPoints: Combines USER_MODE (row/field/sharing enforcement at query time) with stripInaccessible (field sanitation pass)
Explains why SECURITY_ENFORCED's throw-on-violation is wrong for a shared, multi-profile selector
stripInaccessible guarantees field-level sanitation regardless of query-level edge cases
Notes SObjectAccessDecision's visibility into which fields were actually removed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements USER_MODE plus stripInaccessible in the selector
Correctly explains why SECURITY_ENFORCED alone is wrong for a shared selector

questions.title: LWC: Wire Adapter Plus Imperative Apex for a Related-List Component
questions.prompt: Build a Lightning Web Component that displays a related list of Contacts for an Account using the reactive wire service for the initial load, plus an imperative Apex call to refresh after a user action, and explain why both are needed.
questions.modelAnswer: The wire adapter is used for the initial load because it's reactive to changes in recordId and to the Lightning Data Service cache, giving automatic re-fetching when the component's tracked parameter changes and participating in the platform's shared cache so other components reading the same Apex method with the same parameters don't trigger a redundant server round trip. Storing the full wire result object (not just result.data) in wiredContactsResult is deliberate and necessary, because refreshApex() requires the entire wire adapter's provisioned value, including its internal cache key, to correctly invalidate and re-fetch — passing just the data array would not actually refresh anything. The imperative path exists for the add-contact action because wire adapters cannot be invoked on demand in response to an arbitrary user action; they only re-fire when their reactive parameters change, so creating a new Contact requires an imperative Apex call, and critically, that call alone would not update this component's wired data since the wire service has no way to know the underlying data changed from an unrelated imperative call. Calling refreshApex(this.wiredContactsResult) immediately after the imperative create is what closes that gap, forcing the specific wired call to re-execute against the server and refresh the UI with the newly created record, which is the standard and necessary pattern any time an imperative DML operation needs to be reflected in wire-provisioned data.
questions.professionalAnswer: I use wire for the initial load because it's reactive — it automatically refetches when recordId changes, and it plays nicely with the Lightning Data Service cache, so if some other component on the page is asking for the same data, they're not both hitting the server separately. The part that trips people up is storing the whole wire result, not just the data array — refreshApex needs that whole object, cache key included, to actually know what to refresh; if you only keep result.data, calling refreshApex later just does nothing useful. The imperative call is there because wire adapters only refire when their own reactive parameters change — there's no hook for 'the user just clicked a button and created a record,' so creating the Contact has to go through an imperative Apex call. But that imperative call by itself won't update what's on screen, because the wire service has no idea that unrelated call touched the same data — so I always follow it with refreshApex on the stored wire result, which is really the standard move any time you mix an imperative write with wire-provisioned reads.
commonMistakes: Stores only result.data instead of the full wire result object, breaking refreshApex
Assumes the imperative create call automatically updates the wired related list
Tries to call the wire-adapted function imperatively instead of using a separate imperative Apex method
Doesn't call refreshApex at all after the imperative mutation, leaving stale UI
keyPoints: Wire adapter used for reactive initial load, benefiting from LDS caching
Stores the entire wire result (not just .data) to enable refreshApex
Imperative Apex required for on-demand user actions wire adapters can't trigger
refreshApex explicitly called after the imperative mutation to sync the UI

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly implements the reactive wire adapter for initial load
Correctly stores and uses the full wire result for refreshApex
Correctly explains why an imperative call is needed for the user action
Correctly closes the loop with refreshApex after the imperative mutation

questions.title: Testing a Chained Queueable with Test.startTest/stopTest
questions.prompt: Write an Apex test method that correctly exercises a Queueable chain (where execute() enqueues a follow-up job), ensuring both jobs actually run within the test.
questions.modelAnswer: The critical mechanic is that Test.stopTest() forces all asynchronous operations enqueued since the matching Test.startTest() — including any jobs that themselves enqueue further jobs during that synchronous execution — to run to completion before control returns to the test method, which is what allows a single test to actually validate a multi-batch chain rather than only observing the first job's effects. Test.setMock(HttpCalloutMock.class, ...) is required before the chain runs because the Queueable's execute() method performs a real callout, and Apex tests are not permitted to make actual HTTP callouts; without a registered mock the first execute() invocation would throw immediately. Using 120 records with a batch size of 50 is deliberate test design, not an arbitrary number — it guarantees the chain must actually execute at least three times (not just once) to process everything, which is what actually exercises the chaining logic rather than coincidentally passing because everything fit in a single batch. The assertion checks every record across the full original ID set rather than just the first batch, which is the detail that would catch a bug where chaining silently stopped after the first job (a common regression when someone refactors the chaining condition) — asserting only on the first 50 records would pass even with a broken chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mechanic I always lean on is that stopTest doesn't just run the one job you enqueued — it runs everything that job enqueues too, synchronously, before the test method gets control back. That's the only reason a test can validate a multi-hop chain in one shot. I make sure to register an HTTP mock before any of that runs, since this Queueable does a real callout and tests just aren't allowed to make real HTTP calls — skip the mock and the very first execute() blows up. I also picked 120 records against a 50-record batch size on purpose, not randomly — that guarantees the chain actually has to fire more than once to finish, so I'm genuinely testing the chaining, not just getting lucky because everything fit in one batch. And the assertion checks every single record from the original set, not just the first batch, because that's exactly the kind of test that would catch someone accidentally breaking the chain logic in a refactor — if I only checked the first 50, a broken chain would still pass.

Uses a record count that fits entirely in one batch, never actually exercising the chain
Asserts only on the first batch's records instead of the full original ID set
Misunderstands stopTest as running only the directly-enqueued job, not its chained children
keyPoints: Correctly relies on stopTest to synchronously run the entire chain, not just the first job
Registers an HttpCalloutMock before the chain executes its callout
Chooses a record count that forces multiple chain hops
Asserts across the full original record set to catch a silently broken chain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets up the mock callout before running the chain
Correctly relies on stopTest to exercise the full chain
Chooses test data that genuinely forces multiple chain hops

questions.title: Complex SOQL: Relationship Subquery with Aggregate Rollup
questions.prompt: Write a single SOQL query that returns each Account along with the count and total amount of its open Opportunities, without using a separate Apex rollup loop.
questions.code:
SELECT
  Id,
  Name,
  (SELECT Id FROM Opportunities WHERE IsClosed = false).size,
  (
    SELECT Amount
    FROM Opportunities
    WHERE IsClosed = false
  )
FROM Account
WHERE Id IN :accountIds

-- Better: use an aggregate query directly against Opportunity, grouped by Account
SELECT
  AccountId,
  COUNT(Id) openOppCount,
  SUM(Amount) openOppTotal
FROM Opportunity
WHERE IsClosed = false AND AccountId IN :accountIds
GROUP BY AccountId
questions.modelAnswer: The first attempt, a child relationship subquery inline inside the parent SELECT, is a common first instinct but is the wrong tool here: it returns the actual child records (consuming them against the query row limit and sub-query row limits) rather than a scalar, so getting a single count and sum still requires an Apex loop over the returned child records per parent, defeating the goal of avoiding an Apex rollup loop entirely. The correct approach is a direct aggregate query against the child object (Opportunity) with GROUP BY AccountId, using COUNT() and SUM() in the SELECT list, which returns exactly one row per AccountId with the count and total already computed by the query engine — this is both the only way to avoid an Apex-side loop and significantly cheaper at scale, since the aggregation happens inside the database engine rather than by materializing every child record into heap memory first. The tradeoff is that this aggregate query returns AggregateResult rows keyed by AccountId rather than Account records with nested relationship data, so the calling Apex needs a second step (a map keyed by AccountId) to associate each aggregate row back to the Account records it actually needs to act on — but that in-memory map-building is trivial compared to the cost of iterating and manually summing child Opportunity records. For accounts with zero open opportunities, the aggregate query correctly returns no row at all (since GROUP BY only produces rows for groups that exist), so the calling code needs to default any Account not present in the result map to a zero count/sum rather than assuming every requested Account will have a corresponding aggregate row.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct used to be the relationship subquery too, but that's actually the wrong tool for this — it hands back the real child records, which means I'm still looping through them in Apex to get a count and a sum, which is exactly the loop I was trying to avoid in the first place. The right move is a direct aggregate query against Opportunity with GROUP BY AccountId — COUNT and SUM right in the SELECT list — and the database does the aggregation for me, one row per account, no Apex loop needed. The catch is that I get back AggregateResult rows keyed by AccountId, not actual Account records, so I do need a small map-building step afterward to connect those numbers back to the Accounts I actually care about — but that's a trivial loop compared to manually summing child records. And the thing I always warn people about: an account with zero open opportunities just doesn't show up in the aggregate results at all, because GROUP BY only returns groups that exist — so whatever consumes this needs to default missing accounts to zero rather than assuming every account it asked about came back.

Doesn't realize GROUP BY omits accounts with zero matching child records
Forgets to build an AccountId-keyed map to connect aggregate rows back to Account records
Doesn't recognize the performance advantage of database-side aggregation over materializing child records

questions.title: SOSL Multi-Object Search Across Accounts, Contacts, and Cases
questions.prompt: A support console needs a single search box that searches Accounts, Contacts, and Cases simultaneously by a free-text term, returning only a few relevant fields per object. Write the SOSL query.
questions.code:
FIND {Acme*} IN ALL FIELDS
RETURNING
  Account(Id, Name, Industry WHERE Industry != null),
  Contact(Id, FirstName, LastName, Email),
  Case(Id, CaseNumber, Subject, Status WHERE Status != 'Closed')
LIMIT 50
questions.modelAnswer: SOSL, not SOQL, is the correct tool here because the requirement is a single free-text term searched across multiple unrelated object types simultaneously — SOQL can only query one object's field (or its relationships) at a time, while SOSL's FIND clause searches a Salesforce-maintained search index across all specified objects in one call, which is both the only functionally correct approach and far more efficient than issuing three separate LIKE-based SOQL queries. The RETURNING clause scopes each object to only the fields the console actually needs, which matters for both field-level security, performance (less data marshaled back per result) and for keeping the per-object row limits meaningful, since SOSL's default and maximum result limits are shared across the objects requested in the RETURNING clause unless overridden per object. Per-object WHERE clauses inside RETURNING (such as excluding closed Cases) are supported and let the search stay relevant to what a support agent is actually trying to find — surfacing resolved, irrelevant Cases in a live support search would add noise without value. Using IN ALL FIELDS is the broadest, most forgiving search scope for a free-text support search box where the agent might be searching by a name, an email fragment, or a case subject and doesn't know in advance which field the term will match; a narrower scope like IN NAME FIELDS would miss legitimate matches in Case subjects or email addresses.
questions.professionalAnswer: This has to be SOSL, not SOQL — the second you need one search term to hit multiple unrelated objects at once, SOQL just can't do that, it only ever queries one object's data at a time. SOSL's FIND clause searches Salesforce's own search index across everything you list in RETURNING, in one round trip, which also beats running three separate LIKE queries by hand. I always scope RETURNING down to just the fields the UI actually needs — partly for performance, partly because that's what keeps me from accidentally surfacing a field the user shouldn't see. Adding a WHERE inside RETURNING, like filtering out closed Cases, is something I do by default for a live support search — nobody wants to scroll past resolved cases while they're trying to help someone right now. And I go with ALL FIELDS rather than something narrower like NAME FIELDS, because a support agent typing a search term could be matching a name, an email, or a case subject, and I'd rather cast a slightly wider net than silently miss a legitimate match.

Returns every field instead of scoping RETURNING to only what's needed
Uses a narrow search scope (e.g. NAME FIELDS) that misses legitimate matches in other fields
Forgets per-object WHERE clauses can filter irrelevant results like closed Cases

Scopes RETURNING fields per object for security and performance
Uses per-object WHERE clauses to exclude irrelevant results
