questions.title: SOQL with GROUP BY/HAVING for a Duplicate-Detection Governance Report
questions.prompt: Write a SOQL query that a data governance process can run to find all groups of Contacts sharing the same Email address, where more than one Contact uses that email, as a precursor to a dedup review.
questions.code:
SELECT Email, COUNT(Id) duplicateCount
FROM Contact
WHERE Email != null
GROUP BY Email
HAVING COUNT(Id) > 1
ORDER BY COUNT(Id) DESC
LIMIT 200
questions.modelAnswer: GROUP BY Email collapses all Contact rows into one aggregate row per distinct email value, and COUNT(Id) in the SELECT list counts how many Contact records share each grouped email — this is the correct shape for 'find groups sharing a value' rather than a per-record query, which would return every individual Contact rather than the grouped duplicate sets a dedup process actually needs to act on. The WHERE Email != null clause matters because without it, every Contact with a blank email would be grouped together into one enormous 'null' group that the HAVING clause would then flag as the largest duplicate set in the org, which is both meaningless noise for a governance reviewer and would dominate the LIMIT 200 result set, crowding out genuinely actionable duplicate groups. HAVING COUNT(Id) > 1 is the clause that actually implements 'where more than one Contact uses that email' — this has to be a HAVING clause rather than a WHERE clause because the filter is being applied to the aggregated count, which doesn't exist until after grouping, and SOQL (like SQL generally) evaluates WHERE before grouping and HAVING after. Ordering by COUNT(Id) DESC surfaces the highest-impact duplicate groups first within the LIMIT, which matters because a governance reviewer working through this report manually should see the email shared by the most Contacts before working down to borderline two-Contact duplicates.
questions.professionalAnswer: The shape here is GROUP BY Email with a COUNT(Id) alongside it — that collapses everything down to one row per distinct email with a count of how many Contacts share it, which is exactly what a dedup reviewer needs, not a flat list of every Contact. The WHERE Email != null up front is one of those details that's easy to forget but really matters — without it, every Contact with a blank email gets lumped into one giant null group that would show up as the single biggest 'duplicate' in the report, which is just noise crowding out the real duplicates. HAVING COUNT(Id) > 1 is doing the actual filtering work for 'more than one Contact shares this email' — and it has to be HAVING, not WHERE, because the count doesn't exist as a thing to filter on until after the grouping happens. I also sort by the count descending, because if I'm handing this to someone doing manual governance review, I want them hitting the email shared by fifteen Contacts before they get to the ones that are just a two-Contact edge case.
commonMistakes: Uses WHERE COUNT(Id) > 1 instead of HAVING, which is invalid for an aggregated condition
Omits WHERE Email != null, letting blank emails dominate as a false duplicate group
Returns individual Contact records instead of aggregated groups
Doesn't order results, burying the highest-impact duplicate groups in a large result set
keyPoints: Correctly uses GROUP BY plus COUNT to produce aggregated duplicate groups
Excludes null emails to avoid a meaningless dominant null group
Correctly uses HAVING (not WHERE) to filter on the aggregated count
Orders results to surface the highest-impact duplicates first

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly structures the GROUP BY/COUNT aggregation
Correctly excludes null emails from skewing results
Correctly uses HAVING rather than WHERE for the aggregated filter
Orders results usefully for a governance reviewer

questions.title: Designing a CRM Analytics Recipe to Blend Salesforce and External CSV Data
questions.prompt: Walk through the concrete steps of building a CRM Analytics recipe that blends Opportunity data from Salesforce with an externally sourced CSV of regional sales quotas, to produce a dataset showing attainment percentage by region.
questions.modelAnswer: The build starts by connecting the external CSV as a local or external data source — uploaded directly through Data Manager or synced via a connector if it's refreshed on a schedule — and registering it alongside the existing Salesforce Opportunity connection, so both are available as inputs to Data Prep. In the recipe, the first transformation step pulls in the Opportunity object filtered to closed-won records and the relevant date range, then a join (bucket/lookup step) connects Opportunity's region field (or an Account-level region lookup, if region lives on Account rather than Opportunity directly) to the quota CSV's region key, which requires the two region value sets to be normalized to match exactly (e.g., 'US-West' vs. 'West US' would silently fail to join and needs a formula step to reconcile before the join). After the join, a formula/compute step calculates attainment percentage as summed closed-won Amount divided by the quota value from the CSV, grouped and aggregated by region using the recipe's grouping/aggregate transformation, and a final output step registers the resulting dataset for use in a dashboard. The two real failure points to design around are the join-key mismatch (region naming inconsistency between systems) and refresh cadence mismatch — if the CSV is uploaded manually and the Salesforce connection syncs nightly, the dataset will silently reflect out-of-sync quota data until governance establishes a consistent refresh and re-upload process for the external source.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by getting both sources into Data Prep as recipe inputs — the Opportunity data from the existing Salesforce connection, and the quota CSV either uploaded through Data Manager or synced on a schedule if it needs to stay current. Then it's filter Opportunity down to closed-won in the right date range, join it to the quota data on region, aggregate closed-won amount by region, and compute attainment as actual over quota in a formula step before registering the output dataset. The part that actually breaks these in practice, every time, is the join key — if Salesforce says 'US-West' and the CSV says 'West US,' that join just silently fails and you get blank or wrong attainment numbers with no error telling you why. So I always add a normalization step before the join specifically to reconcile naming between the two sources. The other thing I flag early with the business is refresh cadence — if that CSV is a manual upload and the Salesforce side refreshes nightly, this dataset is going to be quietly stale until someone commits to a regular re-upload process, and that's a process problem, not something the recipe itself can fix.
commonMistakes: Doesn't account for region-naming mismatches between the Salesforce data and the external CSV breaking the join
Ignores refresh cadence mismatch between a manually uploaded CSV and a scheduled Salesforce sync
Computes attainment before properly filtering to closed-won/relevant date range, skewing results
Doesn't register/output the final dataset in a form dashboards can actually consume
keyPoints: Connects both the Salesforce object and external CSV as recipe inputs
Normalizes join keys (region naming) before joining the two sources
Correctly sequences filter, join, aggregate, and compute steps
Identifies refresh cadence mismatch as an operational risk, not just a technical one

Identifies and addresses the join-key normalization problem

questions.title: Configuring a Named Credential for an OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials Callout
questions.prompt: Walk through configuring a Named Credential and External Credential for a server-to-server integration using the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials flow, and show the resulting Apex callout.
questions.modelAnswer: Configuration starts with an External Credential set to the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials authentication protocol, where the token endpoint URL, client ID, and client secret are entered as the principal's authentication parameters — critically, the client secret is stored encrypted and never becomes visible again in the UI or retrievable by Apex after it's saved. A Permission Set is then created and assigned to the integration user or to the running context, granting access to that specific External Credential principal, which is what actually authorizes a given Apex execution context to use those credentials rather than every user in the org implicitly having access. The Named Credential itself is created pointing to the actual API base URL and referencing the External Credential for authentication, with the 'Generate Authorization Header' option enabled so the platform automatically requests and caches an access token via the client credentials grant and injects it as a Bearer token on every callout through that Named Credential, handling token expiry and refresh transparently. The resulting Apex code, as shown, never references a URL, client ID, secret, or token at all — it calls callout:Billing_API, and the entire OAuth handshake, token caching, and header injection happens outside Apex, which is precisely the security property that makes Named Credentials the mandated pattern over any hand-rolled HttpRequest-based OAuth implementation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set up the External Credential first, choosing OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials as the protocol and putting the token endpoint, client ID, and secret in there as the principal's parameters — and once that secret's saved, it's gone from view, nobody including me can read it back out of the UI afterward. Then I'd create a Permission Set that grants access to that specific credential and assign it to whichever integration user or context actually needs to make this callout — that's the piece that controls who's allowed to use it, not just where it points. The Named Credential ties the real API URL to that External Credential, and I always turn on automatic header generation so the platform handles getting the token, caching it, and refreshing it before it expires — I don't want to write any of that myself. And that's exactly why the Apex code ends up so boring — it just calls callout:Billing_API with no URL, no secret, no token logic anywhere in sight, which is the whole point: if someone pulls this class into a sandbox or a debug log, there's nothing sensitive in it to leak.

Forgets the Permission Set step, leaving the credential technically configured but inaccessible
Manually implements the OAuth token request/refresh logic in Apex instead of enabling automatic header generation
Doesn't realize the secret becomes unreadable in the UI once saved

Permission Set grants specific access to the credential principal
Named Credential ties the endpoint to the External Credential with automatic header generation
Resulting Apex callout code contains no URL, secret, or token handling at all

Correctly scopes access via a Permission Set

questions.title: Debugging a Mixed DML Exception in a Test Class
questions.prompt: A test class fails intermittently with 'MIXED_DML_OPERATION, DML operation on setup object is not permitted after you have updated a non-setup object.' The test creates a User, then updates an Account, then assigns a Permission Set. Diagnose and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: The root cause is that Salesforce classifies certain objects (User, Group, GroupMember, PermissionSetAssignment, and others related to user/org setup) as 'setup objects,' and within a single transaction, once a non-setup object (Account, in this case) has been inserted or updated, no further DML on a setup object is permitted in that same transaction — this restriction exists because setup-object changes can affect sharing and visibility in ways that could create an inconsistent security state if interleaved with regular data changes mid-transaction. The fix is not to avoid touching setup objects, but to sequence the transaction so that all setup-object DML happens either entirely before or isolated from non-setup DML, typically by wrapping the User creation and PermissionSetAssignment insert inside a System.runAs block, which Apex test context treats as its own transaction boundary separate from the enclosing test method's transaction. Simply reordering the statements (doing all setup-object DML first, then the Account insert) can also resolve it in some cases, but runAs is the more robust fix because it explicitly creates a transaction boundary rather than relying on the implicit single-transaction behavior of a test method, which can be fragile if other setup code is added later and inadvertently interleaves the two DML types again. The intermittent nature of the failure described in the prompt is a strong hint this is exactly this issue — mixed DML errors often only surface depending on exact ordering of setup code that accumulates across a test class over time, which is why isolating setup-object DML in runAs defensively, even when it isn't failing yet, is the safer long-term pattern.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recognize this immediately as the classic setup-object/non-setup-object conflict — Salesforce treats things like User and PermissionSetAssignment as 'setup objects,' and once you've inserted or updated a regular object like Account in the same transaction, you're not allowed to touch a setup object afterward in that same transaction. The fix isn't to stop touching setup objects, it's to isolate that setup-object DML in its own transaction boundary — wrapping the User creation and permission set assignment in a System.runAs block does exactly that. I'd actually flag that the 'intermittent' part of this bug report is a tell — these errors are very sensitive to exact statement ordering, so as test classes grow over time, someone adds one more line of setup and suddenly a previously-passing test starts throwing this. That's exactly why I'd fix it with runAs rather than just reordering the statements — reordering fixes today's failure, but it's fragile the next time someone touches this test; the runAs boundary is the fix that actually holds up.
commonMistakes: Doesn't recognize User/PermissionSetAssignment as setup objects subject to this restriction
Fixes it with simple reordering only, which is fragile against future test changes
Doesn't know System.runAs creates an isolated transaction boundary that resolves this
Assumes the error is random/flaky rather than deterministically tied to DML ordering
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the setup-object vs. non-setup-object DML restriction as the root cause
Explains why mixing them in one transaction throws MIXED_DML_OPERATION
Fixes it by isolating setup-object DML inside a System.runAs transaction boundary
Explains why the failure appears intermittent as the test class grows

questions.title: Diagnosing Recursive Updates Between an After-Save Flow and an Apex Trigger
questions.prompt: After a recent release, updating an Opportunity's Stage field sometimes times out or hits the 'maximum trigger depth' error. An after-save Flow updates a rollup field on Opportunity, and an Apex trigger on Opportunity also updates a different field after save. How do you diagnose and fix the recursion?
questions.modelAnswer: The diagnostic starting point is Setup's Flow interview debug logs combined with Apex debug logs filtered to the trigger, read together in the order they fire, to confirm the actual loop: the after-save Flow updates the Opportunity, which re-triggers the save pipeline including the Apex trigger, and if that Apex trigger's after-update logic also writes back to the Opportunity (even a field the Flow doesn't touch), it re-triggers the Flow again, and this continues until Salesforce's recursion safety limit (16 for both Flow and Apex trigger cumulative recursive invocation in many contexts) throws rather than looping forever — the actual 'maximum trigger depth exceeded' error is the platform protecting itself from what would otherwise be infinite recursion. The fix requires both sides to break the cycle, not just one: either the Apex trigger needs a static recursion guard (a static Boolean or Set<Id> of already-processed record IDs checked and set before the trigger's write-back logic runs) so it only performs its field update once per original transaction even if the trigger context re-fires, or — architecturally cleaner — the logic that currently lives in the after-save Flow should be moved into a before-save flow or into the same Apex trigger if it only needs to set a field on the Opportunity itself, since before-save logic never triggers this re-save cycle at all. The most durable fix is usually to audit whether the after-save Flow's update genuinely needs to be after-save (does it touch other records, send email, or call a subflow with side effects?) — if it's only setting a field on the same Opportunity, it should never have been an after-save flow in the first place, and converting it to before-save eliminates the recursion risk entirely rather than just guarding against it.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd do is pull the Flow interview logs and the Apex debug logs side by side and actually trace the sequence, because 'maximum trigger depth' is the platform telling you it detected a loop and bailed out before it ran forever. What's almost certainly happening is: the after-save Flow updates the Opportunity, that re-save fires the Apex trigger, the trigger's after-update logic writes back to the same record, and that re-triggers the Flow again — round and round until the recursion limit kicks in. The real fix needs to address both sides. On the Apex side, I'd add a static recursion guard so the trigger's write-back only happens once per transaction even if it re-fires. But the fix I actually want is to ask why that Flow logic is after-save in the first place — if all it's doing is setting a field on the same Opportunity record, it should be a before-save flow, full stop, and before-save logic never triggers this re-save cycle at all. That's not just a patch, that's removing the actual cause instead of guarding around it.
commonMistakes: Only adds a recursion guard to one side (Apex or Flow) instead of addressing both or the root cause
Doesn't use Flow interview logs alongside Apex debug logs to actually trace the sequence
Treats the recursion limit error as random/flaky instead of a deterministic loop
Doesn't consider converting the after-save Flow to before-save as the real root-cause fix
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the after-save Flow / Apex trigger mutual re-triggering loop
Uses Flow interview logs plus Apex debug logs together to confirm the sequence
Proposes a recursion guard as an immediate mitigation
Identifies converting the logic to before-save as the durable root-cause fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the recursive after-save/trigger loop

questions.title: Fixing a Queueable Chain That Hits 'Too Many Queueable Jobs'
questions.prompt: A Queueable job chain designed to process a large list in batches is failing in production with 'System.LimitException: Too many queueable jobs added to the queue: 2'. Diagnose the cause and fix the code.
questions.modelAnswer: The rule being violated is that from a synchronous context (trigger, controller, anonymous Apex), only one Queueable job may be enqueued per transaction, but once execution is inside an asynchronous context (a Queueable's own execute method), that single job is permitted to enqueue exactly one more — chaining is allowed, but only one level deep per invocation; what actually causes the 'too many queueable jobs' error is either calling System.enqueueJob more than once within a single execute() invocation, or the chain being kicked off from a context that's already consumed its allowance (for example, enqueuing a Queueable from inside another already-queued job's execute method a second time, or from a context that itself was invoked asynchronously and has less remaining allowance than assumed). The fix is defensive: before chaining, check the actual remaining allowance via Limits.getLimitQueueableJobs() minus Limits.getQueueableJobs() rather than assuming a fixed depth is always available, and if the allowance is exhausted, escalate to a different asynchronous mechanism that doesn't share the same limit — Batch Apex, which has its own separate governance model better suited to processing large lists in bounded chunks regardless of chain depth. This also surfaces a design-level question: a Queueable chain is the wrong tool for genuinely large or unbounded lists in the first place, since it was never designed for indefinite chaining depth the way Batch Apex explicitly was; Queueable chaining is best suited to a small, bounded number of hops (for example, a short post-processing pipeline), and anything resembling 'keep chaining until a large list is exhausted' should usually be Batch Apex from the start.
questions.professionalAnswer: The rule that's getting violated here: from a normal synchronous context you only get to enqueue one Queueable, and once you're inside a Queueable's own execute, you're allowed to chain exactly one more — it's not unlimited depth, and most people assume it is until they hit this exact error. What's likely happening is either enqueueJob getting called more than once in the same execute(), or this chain getting kicked off from a context that already ate into that allowance somewhere upstream. My fix is defensive rather than just 'try again': check the actual remaining queueable allowance before chaining, and if there's none left, fall back to Batch Apex instead of trying to force another queueable hop. But honestly, the bigger conversation I'd have with the team is whether Queueable chaining was ever the right tool for 'keep going until this large list is done' — that's what Batch Apex exists for, with its own governance model built for exactly this. I'd probably recommend migrating this whole pipeline to Batch Apex rather than continuing to patch around Queueable's chaining limits.

Calls System.enqueueJob more than once within a single execute() invocation
Doesn't check remaining queueable allowance before chaining defensively
Doesn't recognize Batch Apex is the better-suited tool for large/unbounded list processing

Diagnoses the actual cause of exceeding that allowance
Applies a defensive check before chaining, with a fallback mechanism

questions.title: Diagnosing an Integration User Hitting API Request Limits
questions.prompt: A nightly integration job between Salesforce and an external ERP has started intermittently failing with 'REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED: TotalRequests Limit exceeded.' The job hasn't changed recently, but order volume has grown. Diagnose root causes and propose fixes.
questions.modelAnswer: The API request limit is a rolling 24-hour total across the entire org for the licensed edition (scaling with the number and type of licenses), shared across every integration, every API-based tool, and every user's API-driven client — so the first diagnostic step is checking Setup's API Usage page (or an EventLogFile of type API) to see whether the integration job itself is consuming disproportionately more calls than before, or whether total org-wide consumption has grown from other sources entirely unrelated to this job, which is a common false attribution when order volume growth gets blamed for a limit that several integrations are actually colliding on. If the job itself is the cause, the most common root cause at growing volume is a per-record API call pattern (one REST call per order rather than a single Bulk API batch, or one callout per record in a loop) that scales linearly with order volume and was tolerable at low volume but becomes the dominant consumer as volume grows — the fix is migrating the integration to the Bulk API (or Bulk API 2.0) for high-volume batch operations, which consumes a small, mostly-flat number of API calls regardless of the number of records in the batch, rather than one call per record. If the root cause is genuinely org-wide — many unrelated integrations and tools sharing the same limit — the fix is either negotiating additional API call allocation with Salesforce (available for Enterprise/Unlimited editions at added cost) or, architecturally, consolidating redundant point-to-point integrations behind an integration layer (middleware or a single service) that can batch and deduplicate calls across what used to be several independently-calling systems. Either way, this is exactly the kind of growth-driven failure that argues for proactive API usage monitoring and alerting at a percentage threshold (e.g., 80% of daily allocation) rather than discovering the problem only once jobs start failing in production.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start in Setup's API Usage page, because this limit is a rolling 24-hour total shared across literally everything hitting the API — every integration, every tool, every API client — so step one is figuring out whether this specific job is actually the thing consuming more calls, or whether total org-wide usage grew from something else entirely and this job is just the one that happened to get throttled. If it's genuinely this job, the usual suspect at growing volume is a one-call-per-record pattern — a REST call per order instead of batching through Bulk API — that was fine at low volume and becomes the dominant consumer as order volume climbs. The fix there is straightforward: move high-volume batch work to Bulk API, which stays roughly flat on API consumption regardless of record count instead of scaling linearly. If it turns out to be genuinely org-wide contention from multiple integrations, then it's either a conversation with Salesforce about additional API allocation, or — the architecturally better answer — consolidating some of those point-to-point integrations behind a shared middleware layer so they're not all independently hammering the same limit. Either way, I'd also push for proactive usage alerting at something like 80% of the daily allocation, because finding out about this from a failed nightly job in production is the worst way to learn it.

Doesn't consider that other integrations sharing the same org-wide limit could be the real cause
Recommends only 'buy more API calls' without considering a Bulk API migration first
No recommendation for proactive monitoring/alerting to catch this before production failure

questions.title: LWC Component Not Refreshing After a Record Update
questions.prompt: Users report that after editing a record via a standard Lightning record edit form, a custom LWC elsewhere on the page showing related summary data doesn't update until a full page refresh. Diagnose and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The most common root cause is that the custom LWC is populating its data via an imperative Apex call (or a wire adapter to a custom Apex method) rather than through Lightning Data Service (getRecord/@wire with a standard field reference), and imperative/custom-Apex-backed data has no automatic subscription to the Lightning Data Service record cache that lightning-record-edit-form and lightning-record-form update when a save occurs — so the edit form's save correctly updates the record in the LDS cache and any component wired to that same record via @wire(getRecord, ...) refreshes automatically, but a component relying on its own Apex call is architecturally disconnected from that cache invalidation entirely. The fix depends on what the custom component's data actually needs: if it can be expressed as fields on the same record (or a few related records reachable via getRelatedListRecords or similar LDS-aware wire adapters), switching the component to use @wire with LDS adapters instead of a custom Apex method makes it automatically reactive to the same cache the edit form updates. If the data genuinely requires custom Apex (a computed aggregate, a cross-object join LDS can't express), the component needs to explicitly listen for the save event — either by firing a Lightning Message Service message or a custom event from the component that performed the edit, or by using the `refreshApex` pattern triggered from a handler on the standard edit form's onsuccess event — rather than relying on any implicit mechanism, since no implicit refresh exists for Apex-backed wire data when an unrelated component elsewhere on the page performs the save. A durable diagnostic check for this exact symptom is confirming whether the component in question actually uses an LDS wire adapter at all; if it's @wire(apexMethod) rather than @wire(getRecord)/@wire(getRelatedListRecords), the lack of auto-refresh is expected, not a bug, and the fix is architectural, not a patch.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nine times out of ten this is because the custom component is pulling its data through its own Apex method rather than through Lightning Data Service — and LDS is specifically the thing that keeps components in sync automatically when a save happens elsewhere on the page. The standard edit form updates the LDS cache directly, so anything wired to @wire(getRecord) picks that up for free; anything wired to a custom Apex method has zero connection to that cache and has no reason to know a save happened anywhere. So the real question is what the component actually needs: if it's just fields on a record LDS can already express, I'd switch it over to an LDS wire adapter and get the auto-refresh for free. If it genuinely needs custom Apex — some aggregate or cross-object logic LDS can't do — then I need to wire up an explicit refresh trigger myself, usually Lightning Message Service to broadcast 'a save happened' or hooking the edit form's onsuccess handler to call refreshApex on the other component. Either way, the fix is architectural, not a patch — this isn't a bug so much as the component being built in a way that was never going to auto-refresh in the first place.
commonMistakes: Assumes any save anywhere on the page should implicitly refresh every other component
Doesn't check whether the affected component uses LDS wire adapters vs. a custom Apex method
Tries to patch this with a timed refresh/polling loop instead of an event-driven fix
Switches to LDS wire adapters even when the data genuinely requires custom Apex logic LDS can't express
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the lack of LDS cache subscription as the root cause
Distinguishes data expressible via LDS wire adapters from genuinely Apex-dependent data
Proposes switching to LDS wire adapters where the data allows it
Proposes an explicit event-driven refresh (LMS or refreshApex) where Apex is genuinely required

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the LDS cache subscription gap as the root cause
Correctly distinguishes LDS-expressible data from Apex-dependent data
Proposes the correct fix for each case
Avoids a non-architectural patch (e.g. polling) as the recommended fix

questions.title: A 2GP Unlocked Package Install Fails on Namespace/Dependency Conflict
questions.prompt: Installing an updated version of an internal 2GP unlocked package into a target org fails with a dependency version error, referencing a second package that the target org already has installed at an older version. Diagnose and resolve.
questions.modelAnswer: 2GP packages declare explicit version dependencies in their sfdx-project.json (packageDirectories' dependencies array), and an install fails this way when the package being installed requires a minimum version of a dependency package that is higher than what's currently installed in the target org — this is the dependency resolution system correctly refusing an install that would otherwise leave the org in an inconsistent state where a component relies on an API or field introduced only in the newer dependency version. The resolution requires first identifying exactly which dependency and version the failing package actually requires (visible in the error detail and in the package's own dependency declaration), then determining whether that dependency package itself has a published, installable newer version that satisfies the requirement — if so, the fix is to install the updated dependency package into the target org first, then retry the original package's installation, which is why dependency packages should always be promoted and installed in dependency order, not just whichever order a release happened to be scripted. If the dependency package's newer version hasn't been released yet, or releasing it has its own blockers, the alternative is to pin the package being installed to an earlier version that doesn't require the newer dependency, accepting the newer features aren't available in that org yet, or to fast-track releasing the dependency update if the business need is urgent. The deeper process fix is a release pipeline that validates the full dependency graph before attempting any installation — CI should fail a release build if its declared dependency versions aren't actually satisfiable in the target environment's current package manifest, rather than discovering the mismatch only at install time in what might be a production deployment window.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the dependency resolution system doing exactly its job — the package I'm installing declares it needs some minimum version of another package, and the target org's currently on an older version than that, so Salesforce is correctly refusing rather than leaving the org in some half-updated, inconsistent state. First thing I'd do is read the actual error to see exactly which dependency and which version it's asking for, then check whether that dependency already has a newer published version I can install first. If it does, the fix is just sequencing — install the dependency update, then retry the original package. If it doesn't have a newer version released yet, I've got two real options: pin the package I'm trying to install to an earlier version that doesn't need the newer dependency, or go fast-track releasing that dependency update if there's real urgency. But honestly, the bigger fix here is process, not this one install — my CI pipeline should be validating the full dependency graph against the target org's actual package manifest before it even lets a release build get this far, so I'm not discovering a version mismatch in the middle of an actual deployment window.
commonMistakes: Doesn't check the package's declared dependency versions in sfdx-project.json before troubleshooting
Installs packages in an arbitrary order rather than resolving dependency order first
Doesn't consider pinning to an earlier compatible version as a valid interim fix
No process-level fix (CI dependency graph validation) proposed to prevent recurrence
keyPoints: Correctly explains why 2GP dependency version mismatches cause install failures
Diagnoses the exact dependency and version required from the error and package declaration
Resolves via correct install ordering or version pinning
Proposes a CI-level fix to validate dependency graphs before release

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the dependency resolution failure mechanism
Correctly diagnoses the specific mismatch from available information
Proposes a correct immediate resolution
Proposes a process-level fix to prevent recurrence

questions.title: A Batch Apex Job Is Hitting CPU Timeout Mid-Run
questions.prompt: A nightly Batch Apex job that processes 200,000 records has started intermittently throwing 'System.LimitException: Apex CPU time limit exceeded' inside its execute() method after an unrelated code change elsewhere added a nested loop over related records. Diagnose and fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The CPU timeout is caused by an O(n*m) nested loop — for every Account in the batch scope (n), the code re-scans the entire allContacts list (m) looking for matches, which means total work scales with n times m rather than n plus m, and CPU time (unlike heap or SOQL limits) accumulates across every line of Apex execution including pure in-memory loop iteration, so a nested scan that was fast enough at a small batch scope size becomes the dominant cost once the related-record change was introduced elsewhere in the codebase increased m (the size of allContacts) without anyone revisiting this loop's complexity. The fix restructures the lookup from a linear re-scan into a single pass that builds a Map<Id, List<Contact>> keyed by AccountId once, after which each Account's related Contacts are retrieved via a single map lookup (O(1) amortized) rather than a full re-scan, converting the overall complexity from O(n*m) to O(n+m) — this is the standard Apex collection pattern (build-a-map-first) that should be the default whenever code needs to repeatedly find records related to another record within an in-memory collection. Because this is a CPU time issue specifically, rather than a SOQL or DML limit, reducing the batch's Scope size in Database.executeBatch would only reduce how much work each individual execute() call does, masking the symptom (fewer timeouts per chunk) without fixing the underlying quadratic algorithm, and the job would still be meaningfully slower in aggregate across all chunks than the corrected linear-time version. Diagnosing this specifically as an algorithmic complexity issue, rather than assuming it requires a batch-size or governor-limit workaround, is the key insight — the fix is in the loop structure, not the batch configuration.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I hear 'intermittent CPU timeout after an unrelated change added a nested loop,' I'm already fairly confident this is an O(n times m) problem, not a governor-limit configuration issue. What's happening is for every Account in the batch, the code re-scans the entire Contact list looking for matches — so total work scales with the product of both list sizes, and CPU time counts every bit of that in-memory loop work, not just SOQL calls. The actual fix is the standard pattern I reach for anytime I need to match records from one in-memory list against another: build a map keyed by the foreign key once, then it's a single map lookup per Account instead of a full re-scan — that turns it from n-times-m work into n-plus-m work, which is a completely different scaling curve. I'd specifically push back on just shrinking the batch's scope size as the fix, because that only reduces how much of this quadratic cost hits any single execute() call — the job as a whole is still doing way more work than it needs to, it'll just fail less obviously while still running slower than it should across the full 200,000 records.
commonMistakes: Treats this as a governor-limit configuration problem and just shrinks the batch scope size
Doesn't identify the nested loop as O(n*m) complexity causing the CPU cost
Fixes only the symptom (timeouts) without addressing the underlying algorithmic inefficiency
Doesn't apply the standard build-a-map-first pattern to convert to linear-time lookup
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the nested loop as O(n*m) algorithmic complexity
Explains that CPU time accumulates across all in-memory execution, not just SOQL/DML
Fixes it with the correct build-a-map-first pattern, converting to O(n+m)
Explains why shrinking batch scope size would mask rather than fix the root cause

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the nested-loop algorithmic complexity as the root cause
Produces a correct map-based linear-time fix

questions.title: A SOQL Query Is Non-Selective Despite Filtering on an Indexed Field
questions.prompt: A report built on a 30-million-row custom object is timing out, even though its underlying query filters on a custom field marked as 'External ID' (which creates a standard index). Diagnose why the query might still be non-selective, and what to check.
questions.code:
-- Query appears indexed but may still be non-selective:
SELECT Id, Name, Status__c
FROM Shipment__c
WHERE External_Order_Id__c LIKE '%2026%'
AND Status__c != 'Cancelled'

-- Leading-wildcard LIKE prevents standard index use.
-- A trailing-wildcard, equality, or IN-based filter can use the index:
SELECT Id, Name, Status__c
FROM Shipment__c
WHERE External_Order_Id__c IN :specificOrderIds
AND Status__c != 'Cancelled'
questions.modelAnswer: An indexed field is not automatically a selective filter; selectivity also depends on the operator used and on the fraction of total rows the filter actually excludes, and the query shown uses a leading-wildcard LIKE ('%2026%'), which cannot use a standard database index at all because a B-tree index can efficiently jump to a starting point for a known prefix but can't do that for a pattern that could match anywhere in the string — the query optimizer in this case falls back to a full table scan across all 30 million rows regardless of the field being marked as an External ID. Beyond the wildcard issue, selectivity thresholds matter even for equality or IN-based filters: Salesforce's query optimizer generally requires a filter to match less than roughly 10% of the total rows (or an absolute threshold around 333,000 records, whichever is smaller) for a custom index to actually be used rather than bypassed in favor of a full scan, so even a properly-indexed, non-wildcard filter on a field where most records share a small number of common values (e.g., Status__c with few distinct values) would still be non-selective. The AND Status__c != 'Cancelled' clause compounds this: a negative/not-equal filter is inherently non-selective because the database can't use an index to efficiently find 'everything except X' the way it can for 'everything equal to X' — so even if the leading-wildcard issue were fixed, this clause alone could still force a full scan if it's the only usable filter. The fix requires both rewriting the LIKE pattern to avoid a leading wildcard (or replacing it with an IN clause against a known, bounded set of exact values, as shown) and checking actual field cardinality/selectivity via Query Plan in Developer Console (the 'Explain plan' feature,) which reports the actual cost and whether an index is being used, rather than assuming the External ID designation alone guarantees a fast query.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing that jumps out to me is that leading-wildcard LIKE — '%2026%' can't use a standard index at all, because a B-tree index can jump straight to a known starting point, but it has no way to efficiently search for a pattern that could be anywhere in the middle of the string. So regardless of that field being marked External ID, this specific query is doing a full scan across all thirty million rows. But even past that, I wouldn't stop there — indexed doesn't automatically mean selective. Salesforce's optimizer generally only uses a custom index if the filter's actually going to exclude something like 90% of the rows; if Status values are mostly concentrated in a few buckets, or if a not-equal filter like this Status__c != 'Cancelled' is the only other thing to lean on, that's inherently non-selective too, because the database can't use an index to efficiently express 'everything except this one value.' My actual diagnostic step, beyond just reading the query, is pulling up Query Plan in Developer Console — it'll tell me the real cost and whether an index is actually being used, instead of me guessing based on field metadata alone. And the fix here is rewriting that LIKE into something index-friendly, like an IN clause against known exact order IDs, not just hoping the External ID flag does the work for me.
commonMistakes: Assumes an indexed field automatically guarantees query selectivity
Doesn't recognize that a leading-wildcard LIKE prevents standard index usage entirely
Doesn't check actual field value distribution/cardinality before trusting the index
Doesn't use Query Plan/Explain Plan in Developer Console to verify actual index usage
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the leading-wildcard LIKE as preventing index usage
Explains that selectivity depends on filter operator and value distribution, not just indexing
Identifies the compounding effect of a non-equality (!=) filter
Recommends Query Plan/Explain Plan to verify actual index usage rather than assuming

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the leading-wildcard LIKE issue
Correctly explains selectivity thresholds beyond mere indexing
Identifies the compounding non-equality filter issue
Recommends the correct diagnostic tool (Query Plan)

questions.title: Sharing Recalculation Takes Hours After a Role Hierarchy Change
questions.prompt: After a planned role hierarchy restructuring affecting 500 users, sharing recalculation on a 50-million-row custom object has been running for over four hours and users are reporting they can't see records they should now have access to. Diagnose and respond.
questions.modelAnswer: The immediate diagnosis is straightforward: a role hierarchy change of this scale on an object this large triggers a full sharing recalculation across every affected record, and that recalculation genuinely can take hours on a 50-million-row object — the users' inability to see records isn't necessarily a bug, it's the expected (if painful) state while recalculation is still in progress, since access grants from the new role structure aren't live until the recalc actually finishes processing each record. The first action is checking the recalculation's actual status, which for sharing rules can be monitored via the 'Sharing Settings' or by checking for an active 'Recalculate Group Membership and Sharing' job in the Setup Jobs area, or opening a case with Salesforce Support for visibility into async sharing recalc jobs that aren't otherwise surfaced in the UI — jumping to remediation before confirming the job is actually still running (rather than stalled or failed) risks taking an action that conflicts with an in-progress recalculation. If the job is confirmed to be running normally and simply large, the honest answer to leadership and affected users is that this was foreseeable and should have been handled with deferred sharing calculation requested from Salesforce Support before the role change was executed, batching the restructuring into the maintenance window rather than triggering recalculation live against production traffic — this is the fix for the next role change, not this one, since deferred sharing calculation has to be arranged in advance of the triggering change, not retroactively. For the current incident, the realistic options are to let the recalculation complete while communicating an accurate ETA to affected users (if Salesforce Support can provide one), or, if the job appears genuinely stalled rather than slow, escalate directly to Salesforce Support since recalculation at this scale isn't something an admin can meaningfully retry or cancel safely once in flight.
questions.professionalAnswer: First thing I'd say, even though it's not what people want to hear: on a 50-million-row object, a role hierarchy change touching 500 users is genuinely a multi-hour recalculation, and users not seeing the right records yet might just mean the recalc hasn't reached those records, not that something's broken. So before I do anything else, I'm checking whether that recalculation job is actually still running and making progress, versus stalled — that usually means looking at what visibility Setup gives me, and if that's not enough, opening a case with Support, because async sharing recalc at this scale isn't always fully visible to an admin. If it's running normally and it's just big, then the honest conversation with leadership is: this was foreseeable, and the right move would've been requesting deferred sharing calculation from Support before the role change went out, so this got batched during a maintenance window instead of recalculating live in production. That's not a fix for right now, though — that has to be arranged ahead of the triggering change, not after. For the actual incident in front of me, it's either let it finish and communicate a realistic timeline, or escalate to Support directly if it looks genuinely stuck, because this isn't something I can safely cancel or retry myself once it's in flight.
commonMistakes: Assumes something is broken rather than first confirming this is expected recalculation time at this scale
Attempts to cancel or retry the recalculation without understanding the risk of doing so mid-flight
Doesn't mention deferred sharing calculation as the preventive fix that should have been requested beforehand
Can't distinguish between 'running normally but large' and 'genuinely stalled' as different situations needing different responses
keyPoints: Correctly recognizes multi-hour recalculation as plausible/expected at this scale, not automatically a bug
Checks actual job status before taking remediation action
Identifies deferred sharing calculation as the preventive fix that should have preceded the change
Gives a realistic, scale-appropriate response for the current in-flight incident

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assesses whether this is expected behavior at scale vs. a genuine failure
Describes a correct diagnostic approach to check job status
Identifies deferred sharing calculation as the preventive measure for next time

questions.title: A Data Migration Load Fails on Parent-Child Lookup Resolution Order
questions.prompt: A large data migration loading Accounts, Contacts, and Opportunities (with Opportunities referencing both Account and Contact via lookups) is failing partway through with a high rate of lookup resolution errors. Diagnose the likely cause and the correct fix.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that the load isn't sequencing inserts in proper dependency order, or isn't using external IDs to resolve cross-object lookups, so child records (Opportunities) are being loaded before their parent records (Accounts, Contacts) exist in the target org, or are attempting to resolve a lookup using the source system's internal record ID rather than a stable external ID field mapped in the target — Salesforce record IDs are generated on insert and are different from whatever ID the legacy source system used, so any load step referencing 'the old system's Account ID' directly instead of through an External ID field marked as such on the target Account object will fail to resolve. The correct fix requires loading objects in strict parent-to-child dependency order (Accounts first, then Contacts referencing those Accounts, then Opportunities referencing both), and for each parent object, populating an indexed External ID field with the legacy system's identifier so that child-record loads can reference that external ID directly in the lookup field during insert (most bulk load tools, and the Bulk API itself, support this upsert-by-external-ID pattern natively), rather than requiring a separate ID-mapping lookup step maintained manually. For cases where true circular or co-dependent references exist (for example, an Account's primary Contact lookup pointing to a Contact that itself needs to reference that Account), the standard technique is a two-pass load: insert both objects with the problematic lookup left blank in the first pass, then run a second update pass that populates the cross-reference now that both sides have valid external IDs to resolve against. Beyond the immediate fix, this failure pattern indicates the migration plan itself should have explicitly documented a dependency-ordered load sequence and external ID strategy before execution began, since discovering lookup resolution order problems mid-load on a large object risks partial, inconsistent data that then needs careful reconciliation rather than a clean re-run.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess is a load-ordering problem, maybe combined with not using external IDs properly. Opportunities are trying to resolve lookups to Accounts and Contacts, and if those parent records haven't been loaded yet, or if the load is trying to match on the legacy system's internal ID instead of a mapped External ID field on the target object, those lookups are just going to fail to resolve. The fix is to load strictly in dependency order — Accounts, then Contacts, then Opportunities — and to populate an external ID field on each parent object with the legacy system's identifier, so the child loads can reference that external ID directly during insert rather than needing some separate ID-mapping step maintained by hand. If there's a genuine circular reference — say an Account pointing to its primary Contact, and that Contact pointing back to the Account — I'd handle that with a two-pass load: insert both sides with that one lookup left blank first, then run an update pass afterward once both records have valid external IDs to resolve against. But stepping back, the real lesson here is that this should have been caught in planning, not discovered mid-load — a migration plan for a multi-object load like this needs an explicit dependency order and external ID strategy written down before anyone runs it, because partial failures on a large load leave you with inconsistent data that's a lot more painful to reconcile than just fixing the plan and re-running cleanly.
commonMistakes: Loads objects out of dependency order (children before parents)
Attempts to resolve lookups using the legacy system's internal ID instead of a mapped External ID field
Doesn't have a plan for genuinely circular/co-dependent references (two-pass load)
Treats this as a one-off load bug rather than a planning gap in the migration strategy
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses load-order and/or external-ID resolution as the root cause
Prescribes strict parent-to-child dependency load ordering
Prescribes using External ID fields for lookup resolution during bulk load
Describes the two-pass technique for genuinely circular references

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the load-order/external-ID root cause
Prescribes correct dependency-ordered loading
Prescribes correct External ID-based lookup resolution
Addresses circular reference handling and migration planning

questions.title: A CRM Analytics Dataflow Times Out on a Large Nightly Sync
questions.prompt: A CRM Analytics dataflow that syncs and transforms a large Opportunity dataset nightly has started timing out as the underlying object has grown past several million rows. Diagnose likely causes and propose fixes.
questions.modelAnswer: CRM Analytics dataflows and recipes have their own processing time and complexity ceilings that scale with both row count and the number/complexity of transformation steps (joins, augments, compute expressions chained together), so a dataflow that completed comfortably within its nightly window at a smaller row count can begin timing out purely from organic data growth even with zero changes to the dataflow's logic. The first diagnostic step is checking the dataflow's execution monitoring (Data Manager's monitor view) to identify which specific node or step is consuming the most time, since the fix differs meaningfully depending on whether the bottleneck is the initial digest/extract step (often fixable by moving to incremental extraction rather than a full digest every run), an expensive join/augment step against another large dataset (often fixable by filtering or pre-aggregating one side of the join before the augment rather than joining the full unfiltered datasets), or a late compute-expression step doing row-level logic that could be pushed earlier or simplified. A high-value, commonly underused fix is switching the extract step from a full sync to an incremental one where the source data supports a reliable 'last modified' watermark, since re-processing the entire multi-million-row object from scratch every night is often the single largest avoidable cost once the object has grown past the point where a full nightly digest fits comfortably in the processing window. If the dataflow genuinely needs the full transformation complexity and incremental extraction isn't sufficient on its own, migrating the logic to a recipe (if it's still a legacy dataflow) can help since recipes benefit from newer optimizations in the underlying execution engine, and splitting one large dataflow into multiple smaller, independently-scheduled dataflows/recipes that each handle a narrower slice of the transformation can also reduce any single job's time below the timeout threshold even if total processing time across all of them doesn't shrink.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd say is: this might not be a bug at all, it might just be organic growth running into a fixed processing ceiling that scales with row count and transformation complexity — a dataflow that was comfortably fast at a smaller row count can start timing out with zero logic changes just because the object grew. So I'd go straight to the dataflow's monitor view in Data Manager to see which specific node is actually eating the time, because the fix is different depending on whether it's the initial extract, an expensive join, or a late compute step. The fix I'd look at first, and the one people skip most often, is switching from a full nightly digest to an incremental extract if there's a reliable last-modified field to key off of — reprocessing the entire multi-million-row object from scratch every single night is usually the biggest avoidable cost once an object's grown past a certain size. If that's not enough on its own, I'd look at whether this is still a legacy dataflow that could move to a recipe to pick up newer engine optimizations, and as a last resort, splitting one big dataflow into a few smaller, independently scheduled ones so no single job alone breaches the timeout, even if the total work across all of them doesn't actually shrink.
commonMistakes: Assumes the timeout is a bug rather than organic scale outgrowing a fixed processing ceiling
Doesn't use the dataflow monitor view to identify the actual bottleneck node
Doesn't consider incremental extraction as the highest-value fix for a full nightly re-digest
Jumps straight to splitting the dataflow without first checking for a simpler extraction-level fix
keyPoints: Correctly frames this as a scale-driven ceiling, not necessarily a logic bug
Uses dataflow monitoring to identify the actual bottleneck node/step
Identifies incremental extraction as the highest-value fix where applicable
Considers recipe migration and job splitting as further mitigations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the timeout as a scale-driven issue, not assumed logic bug
Uses the correct diagnostic tool to isolate the bottleneck
Proposes incremental extraction as the primary high-value fix
Proposes valid further mitigations (recipe migration, job splitting)

questions.title: Division Field Misconfiguration Causing Missing Records in Reports
questions.prompt: An org with Divisions enabled has reports that are mysteriously missing records that users confirm exist and that they have access to via sharing. Diagnose the likely cause related to the Division field.
questions.modelAnswer: The Division field implicitly scopes reports and list views to the user's currently selected 'working division' (set in their personal settings) unless the report or view is explicitly configured to show 'All Divisions,' so the most common cause of this exact symptom is users running reports while their working division is set to a specific division, silently filtering out legitimately accessible records that happen to belong to a different division — this is independent of and unrelated to sharing access entirely, which is why users confirming they have sharing access to the missing records is a red herring that doesn't rule out the Division filter as the cause. The fix for an individual report is checking and explicitly setting the report's Division filter to 'All Divisions' rather than leaving it defaulted to the running user's current working division, and if this is a widespread problem across many reports and many users, the better fix is auditing report folder-level or org-wide default report filter settings and standard report types to ensure Division filtering defaults to 'All Divisions' for roles that genuinely need a cross-division view, rather than relying on each user to remember to change it per report. A second, less common but related cause is records being assigned to the wrong Division at creation time (if the Division assignment default or an automation setting it has a bug), which would cause records to be systematically miscategorized and excluded from division-scoped views even when every other configuration is correct — this is distinguished from the first cause by checking the actual Division field value on a specific missing record directly, which if it doesn't match what's expected points to a data/assignment problem rather than a report-filter problem. Given how rarely Divisions are used in modern orgs, this is also a good moment to ask whether the org still has a genuine business need for Divisions at all, since many orgs that enabled it years ago for a reason that no longer applies would be better served by disabling the feature and relying on sharing rules and record types instead, which eliminates this entire class of confusing symptom.
questions.professionalAnswer: The Division field quietly filters reports to the user's current working division unless the report is explicitly set to 'All Divisions' — and that's completely separate from sharing. So the fact that users say they have sharing access to the missing records doesn't rule this out at all; it's actually a strong hint, because sharing access and division-based report filtering are two unrelated mechanisms, and a record can be fully shared with someone and still get filtered out of their report by their current working division setting. The fix for one report is just checking its Division filter and setting it to All Divisions instead of leaving it on whatever the user's default working division happens to be. If this is happening across a lot of reports, I'd rather fix it at the report-type or folder-default level so people aren't relying on remembering to flip that setting every single time. I'd also just directly check the Division value on one of the actual missing records, because if it's not what anyone expected, that points to a data assignment bug rather than a report-filter issue — those need different fixes. And honestly, given how rarely orgs genuinely need Divisions anymore, I'd also ask whether this org still has a real reason to keep it enabled — a lot of the time the answer is no, and turning it off removes this whole category of confusing symptom permanently.
commonMistakes: Assumes sharing access rules out the Division field as a cause, when the two are unrelated mechanisms
Fixes only the one report's Division filter without checking for a widespread report-type/default issue
Doesn't distinguish a report-filter cause from a record-assignment (wrong Division value) cause
Doesn't consider whether the org still has a genuine need for Divisions at all
keyPoints: Correctly explains the Division field's implicit report/list-view scoping behavior
Correctly identifies that sharing access is unrelated to Division filtering
Distinguishes a report-filter cause from a record-level Division assignment cause
Questions whether the org still needs Divisions enabled at all

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the Division field's implicit scoping behavior on reports
Correctly separates this from sharing-based access
Distinguishes report-filter vs. record-assignment causes

questions.title: A dbt Model Change Breaks a Reverse-ETL Sync into Salesforce
questions.prompt: A dbt model that feeds a reverse-ETL sync into a Salesforce custom object was changed to rename a column for clarity. The next sync run fails outright, and records that previously synced successfully stop updating. Diagnose and propose a fix and a longer-term prevention.
questions.modelAnswer: The immediate cause is a broken contract: the reverse-ETL tool's field mapping configuration references the dbt model's output column by its exact name, and renaming that column in the dbt model changes the model's output schema without the reverse-ETL sync's mapping being updated to match, so the sync either fails outright looking for a column that no longer exists, or — more dangerously in a less strict tool — silently maps nothing to the destination field, which stops updates without throwing an obvious error. The immediate fix is restoring the sync by either reverting the column rename or updating the reverse-ETL mapping configuration to reference the new column name, whichever is faster to deploy safely, paired with a manual re-run of the sync to catch up any records that should have updated during the outage window. The durable prevention is establishing a contract between the dbt model and its downstream consumers: dbt model contracts (enforced column names and types) on any model that feeds a reverse-ETL sync or another downstream system turn a silent or late-discovered breaking change into a CI-time failure when someone tries to merge the rename, and documenting in the model's YAML that it has an external consumer (via a simple tag or description) gives the next developer a signal to check before renaming anything, since dbt itself has no built-in awareness of consumers living outside the warehouse. This failure pattern is a specific instance of a more general governance gap worth raising with the team: any model feeding a system outside the warehouse (reverse ETL, an API, a scheduled export) needs to be treated with the same change-management discipline as a public API contract, because the blast radius of a 'just a rename' change is invisible from inside dbt alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: What broke here is a contract nobody wrote down: the reverse-ETL tool's field mapping points at the dbt model's output column by its exact name, and renaming that column changed the model's output without anyone updating that mapping to match — so the sync either errors out looking for a column that's gone, or in a less strict setup, just quietly stops mapping anything into that field, which is honestly the scarier failure because nothing obviously breaks, it just stops updating. The immediate fix is just restoring the contract — either revert the rename or update the mapping to the new name, whichever ships faster — and then manually re-running the sync to catch up whatever should have updated during the gap. But the fix I actually care about is preventing this from happening again: putting a dbt model contract on anything that feeds a reverse-ETL sync, so a breaking rename fails in CI when someone tries to merge it, not three hours later in a production sync job. I'd also just tag or document in the model's YAML that it has an external consumer, because dbt itself has no idea anything outside the warehouse is depending on that column name — that context has to live somewhere a future developer will actually see it before they casually rename something for clarity.

questions.title: Multi-Org Strategy: When to Split vs. Consolidate
questions.prompt: A company that grew through acquisition now runs four separate Salesforce orgs, one per acquired business unit, with duplicated customer records across orgs and no unified reporting. Leadership asks you, as the architect, whether to consolidate into one org or formalize a multi-org strategy instead. Walk through how you'd actually make this decision and design the resulting architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: This decision is never purely technical — it hinges on how independently the business units actually need to operate (different sales processes, different regulatory regimes, different release cadences) versus how much they genuinely need a unified customer view, and a good architect resists leadership's implicit assumption that 'one org' is automatically the mature end state. A single consolidated org gives one source of truth, eliminates duplicate licensing and integration overhead, and simplifies reporting, but it forces every business unit onto the same object model, the same release calendar, and the same security model, which is a real cost if the units have genuinely divergent processes or compliance needs (e.g., one unit under different data residency requirements). A deliberate multi-org strategy keeps units independent where that independence is a genuine business asset, but requires actively designing the things a single org gives for free: a master data management layer (often outside Salesforce, e.g., in a warehouse or a dedicated MDM tool) to deduplicate and unify customer records across orgs, and cross-org reporting built either through that external layer or through Salesforce-to-Salesforce/cross-org data sharing tools, rather than hoping four independent orgs will somehow produce one coherent view by accident. The actual decision process starts with a structured assessment, not a default preference: document each business unit's process divergence, compliance requirements, and expected integration points, then weight those against the organizational cost of forcing convergence, and treat 'consolidate' and 'multi-org with explicit MDM/reporting' as two legitimate architectures to choose between on the evidence, not a maturity ladder where consolidation is always the answer. For four orgs from historical acquisitions specifically, the sign that consolidation is probably eventually right is if the four units are *converging* commercially (shared customers, cross-sell motion, unified sales org), whereas the sign that formalized multi-org is right is if the units remain genuinely distinct businesses that leadership has no intention of operationally merging — in which case the investment belongs in MDM and cross-org reporting, not in a disruptive, multi-year single-org migration that doesn't actually serve a converging business reality.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell leadership directly that 'one org' isn't automatically the grown-up answer here — it's a real tradeoff, and the right call depends on whether these four business units are actually converging as a business or staying genuinely distinct. If they're starting to share customers and cross-sell, a single org pays for itself fast: one source of truth, no duplicate licensing, reporting that just works. But if these are four businesses leadership has no real intention of operationally merging, forcing them onto one object model and one release calendar is a cost with no matching benefit, and formalizing a multi-org strategy is the more honest architecture — as long as I actually build the two things a single org gives you for free: a real MDM layer to dedupe and unify customer records across the four orgs, and cross-org reporting that doesn't rely on someone manually stitching four exports together. So my actual process is: go document how divergent these four units really are — process, compliance, who owns which customers — and let that evidence pick the architecture, rather than defaulting to 'more consolidation is always more mature.' And if I do find real convergence, I'd be honest that a multi-year single-org migration is disruptive and only worth proposing if the business reality actually supports it.

Recommends multi-org without designing an MDM/dedup layer or cross-org reporting solution
Treats the decision as purely technical, ignoring process divergence and compliance drivers
Doesn't propose a structured assessment process, just an opinion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames this as a genuine tradeoff, not a maturity ladder

deepDive.heading: Reframe the question leadership actually asked
deepDive.content: Leadership framed this as 'should we consolidate,' which already assumes consolidation is the destination and multi-org is just a temporary, immature state. The first job as architect is to reframe this as a genuine two-way decision: formalized multi-org, done deliberately with the right supporting architecture, is a legitimate end state for a business that genuinely operates as distinct units — not a failure to eventually fix. Accepting the leading framing and jumping straight to a consolidation plan skips the actual decision that needs to be made.

deepDive.heading: Build the real decision matrix
deepDive.content: The decision rests on three axes, assessed per business unit against the others: process divergence (do the four units run meaningfully different sales/service processes, or are they converging on shared ones?), compliance/regulatory divergence (data residency, industry-specific regulation that would force separate data handling regardless of org structure), and commercial convergence (shared customers, cross-sell motion, a sales org starting to operate across unit boundaries). High divergence on the first two and low convergence on the third points toward formalized multi-org. Low divergence and high convergence points toward consolidation. Mixed signals — which is common post-acquisition — point toward a phased approach: consolidate the units that are converging first, leave genuinely distinct units on separate orgs.

deepDive.heading: Design the multi-org support layer (if that's the outcome)
deepDive.content: A deliberate multi-org strategy is only legitimate if it actively replaces what a single org gives for free. That means a master data management layer — typically outside Salesforce, in a warehouse (e.g., Snowflake) with dbt-modeled deduplication logic, or a dedicated MDM tool — that ingests customer records from all four orgs via CDC or Bulk API, applies deterministic and probabilistic matching to resolve duplicate customer identities across orgs, and publishes a canonical customer ID that each org can optionally store back (via reverse ETL) for cross-referencing. Cross-org reporting is built on top of that same unified layer, not by trying to stitch together four live Salesforce connections at report-run time.

deepDive.heading: Design the consolidation path (if that's the outcome)
deepDive.content: If the evidence points toward consolidation, it should be phased, not big-bang: pick the unit with the simplest process and least divergent compliance needs to migrate first, proving the unified object model and migration tooling (data migration architecture: external-ID-based, dependency-ordered loads) on the lowest-risk unit before tackling the most complex one. Each migration wave needs its own LDV and sharing-model plan, since merging four units' data into one object set changes volume and access patterns substantially. Business process differences that can't be reconciled should be modeled as record types and page layouts within the single org, not forced into false uniformity.

deepDive.heading: Governance regardless of outcome
deepDive.content: Whichever architecture is chosen, a governance body (an architecture review board spanning the business units) needs to own the decision criteria going forward — the next acquisition shouldn't restart this debate from scratch. Documenting the decision matrix and its outcome as a standing reference gives future architects a template rather than a one-off analysis that gets lost.

deepDive.heading: Common failure modes to flag to leadership
deepDive.content: The two failure modes to explicitly warn leadership about: consolidating purely for the appearance of maturity without actual commercial convergence, which produces years of disruptive migration for no real business benefit; and declaring 'multi-org strategy' without ever actually building the MDM and cross-org reporting layer, which just leaves the original duplicated-records problem permanently unsolved under a more official-sounding name.

questions.title: Layered Apex Architecture for a Large, Multi-Team Dev Org
questions.prompt: A company with 15 Apex developers across three scrum teams working in the same org has accumulating merge conflicts, duplicated logic, and inconsistent patterns. Propose an enterprise Apex architecture that would actually solve this at the team-structure level, not just a coding-standards document.
questions.modelAnswer: A layered fflib-style architecture (selectors, domains, services, with a clear dependency direction — services depend on domains and selectors, domains depend on selectors, nothing depends upward) solves the duplication problem structurally rather than through a style guide, because logic that would otherwise get reimplemented by each team lives in exactly one place regardless of which team touches it next. The merge-conflict problem is addressed by organizing the codebase (and ideally the deployment units, via 2GP unlocked packages) around domain boundaries that roughly map to the three scrum teams' areas of ownership, so each team primarily works within its own domain/service/selector classes and package, and cross-team changes become explicit package-dependency updates reviewed at a boundary rather than silent collisions inside a single shared monolith of Apex files. An architecture review board or a lighter-weight technical lead sync should own approval of any change that crosses a domain boundary (a new dependency between packages, or a shared utility class multiple teams need), which prevents the common failure mode where layering exists on paper but every team quietly reaches past the boundary when a deadline is tight. The approach also needs a shared 'core' package for genuinely cross-cutting concerns (a trigger handler framework, a generic logging utility, custom exception types) that is explicitly owned by one team or a rotating architecture guild rather than being everyone's problem and therefore no one's, since an unowned shared package is where inconsistent patterns actually creep back in even after the initial reorganization.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell this team that a coding standards doc alone won't fix this, because the actual problem is structural — fifteen developers across three teams are all reaching into the same shared pile of Apex files, so of course you get merge conflicts and duplicated logic. The real fix is a layered architecture — selectors, domains, services — organized around domain boundaries that roughly match how the three scrum teams are actually split, ideally packaged as separate 2GP unlocked packages so each team's day-to-day work mostly lives inside their own package instead of one shared monolith. Cross-team changes then become an explicit package dependency update that gets reviewed at a boundary, instead of three people silently colliding inside the same file. I'd also insist on a genuinely owned shared 'core' package for things like the trigger handler framework or logging utilities — if that's everyone's responsibility, it ends up being no one's, and that's exactly where I've seen inconsistent patterns creep right back in even after a team does the work to reorganize everything else.

Doesn't organize domain/package boundaries around actual team ownership
Leaves cross-cutting shared code unowned, allowing inconsistency to creep back in
No governance mechanism for approving changes that cross domain boundaries
