questions.title: Choosing Between REST, Bulk, Streaming, and Pub/Sub API
questions.prompt: Walk through the real decision criteria for choosing among REST API, Bulk API, Platform Events over Pub/Sub API, and CDC for four different integration scenarios: (1) a mobile app reading a single record on demand, (2) a nightly load of two million order records from an ERP, (3) notifying a fulfillment system the instant an order is approved, (4) keeping an external data warehouse in sync with all Account changes.
questions.modelAnswer: For the mobile app reading a single record on demand (scenario 1), REST API is correct because the interaction is synchronous, low-volume, and latency-sensitive — a user is waiting on screen for a response, and REST's request/response model with per-call overhead that's negligible at this volume is exactly fit for purpose; Bulk API would add unacceptable latency for a single-record read, and an event-based approach doesn't fit a pull-on-demand access pattern at all. For the nightly ERP load of two million records (scenario 2), Bulk API (or Bulk API 2.0) is correct because its asynchronous, chunked, parallel-processing design is built specifically for high-volume batch operations, and using REST for two million individual record calls would both be dramatically slower and would consume a crippling fraction of the org's rolling 24-hour API call allocation, since each REST call counts as one request while Bulk API batches cost far fewer calls regardless of record count. For the instant fulfillment notification (scenario 3), a custom Platform Event published over the Pub/Sub API is correct because this is a business event requiring low-latency, real-time delivery to a subscriber, with a durable, replayable event stream that Pub/Sub API provides as the modern, gRPC-based successor to the legacy CometD/Streaming API, giving at-least-once delivery semantics and a 24-hour (or higher-tier) retention window for replay if the subscriber was briefly offline. For keeping a warehouse in sync with all Account changes (scenario 4), Change Data Capture is correct because the requirement is exhaustive field-level change tracking on a standard object with no custom business logic about which changes matter, and CDC's automatic publish-on-change behavior over the same Pub/Sub API infrastructure, combined with its gap-resilient replay capability, is purpose-built for exactly this kind of change-feed-to-warehouse pattern (often consumed via a connector like a CDC-aware ETL tool) rather than requiring a nightly Bulk API full extract that would miss intra-day changes and waste processing on unchanged records.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through these one at a time with the actual shape of the problem, not a one-size-fits-all rule. The mobile app reading one record on demand is REST, straightforwardly — it's synchronous, low volume, and the user's sitting there waiting, so you want the lowest-latency request/response tool, not something batch-oriented. The nightly two-million-record ERP load is Bulk API, full stop — REST would be painfully slow at that volume and would eat a huge chunk of the org's daily API call budget, since Bulk API batches cost far fewer calls than one-call-per-record. The instant fulfillment notification is a custom Platform Event over Pub/Sub API — that's a business event that needs real-time, durable, replayable delivery, which is exactly what Pub/Sub API is built for, as the modern replacement for the old CometD streaming approach. And keeping a warehouse in sync with every Account change is Change Data Capture — that's exhaustive field-level tracking with no business logic deciding what matters, which is precisely CDC's job, and it beats a nightly full Bulk extract because it won't miss anything that happened intra-day and won't waste processing re-pulling records that didn't actually change.

deepDive.heading: Establish the decision axes before picking a tool
deepDive.content: Before mapping any scenario to an API, name the axes that actually drive the decision: latency requirement (is a human or system waiting synchronously, or is eventual delivery fine?), volume (single record vs. millions), whether the trigger is a raw data change or a business-meaningful condition, and whether durable replay matters (can the consumer tolerate missing an event if it's briefly offline?). Every one of the four scenarios resolves cleanly once these axes are made explicit, and most wrong answers in interviews come from skipping straight to a tool name without walking through them.

deepDive.heading: Scenario 1 — REST API for on-demand mobile reads
deepDive.content: Low volume, synchronous, latency-sensitive, no replay need (the mobile app just re-requests if it misses something). REST's per-call overhead is irrelevant at this volume, and its request/response model directly matches a user waiting on screen. Any event-based or batch tool would be the wrong shape entirely — this isn't a push problem, it's a pull problem.

deepDive.heading: Scenario 2 — Bulk API for the nightly ERP load
deepDive.content: Two million records is firmly in Bulk API territory: it processes data asynchronously in parallel-executed batches server-side, and critically, API call consumption scales with the number of batches, not the number of records, which is the deciding factor against REST at this volume — two million REST calls would both be slow and would likely exceed or dominate the org's rolling 24-hour API limit on their own. Bulk API 2.0 specifically simplifies the chunking/polling that the original Bulk API required the caller to manage directly.

deepDive.heading: Scenario 3 — Platform Events over Pub/Sub API for real-time business events
deepDive.content: 'The instant an order is approved' is a business condition, not a raw field change, so it needs a custom Platform Event (with Apex or Flow logic deciding when 'approved' truly means approved) rather than CDC. Pub/Sub API is the delivery mechanism — a gRPC-based, high-throughput, bidirectional streaming API that replaced the older CometD-based Streaming API for both Platform Events and CDC, offering at-least-once delivery and a retention window that allows a temporarily offline subscriber to catch up via replay rather than losing the event.

deepDive.heading: Scenario 4 — Change Data Capture for exhaustive warehouse sync
deepDive.content: 'All Account changes' with no selection logic is the textbook CDC use case: enabling CDC on Account publishes a change event automatically for every create/update/delete/undelete, over the same Pub/Sub API infrastructure, with a payload that includes which fields changed. This is architecturally superior to a nightly Bulk API full extract for this requirement because it captures intra-day changes immediately and avoids reprocessing unchanged records — the warehouse-side consumer (often a CDC-aware connector) applies these as incremental upserts rather than needing a nightly full reconciliation.

deepDive.heading: Why conflating scenario 3 and 4 is the most common mistake
deepDive.content: Both scenario 3 and 4 use the same underlying Pub/Sub API transport, which is exactly why candidates conflate them. The distinguishing question is always: does publishing require business logic to decide if/when (Platform Event), or does every raw change qualify automatically (CDC)? Getting this distinction right, not just naming the right API, is what actually demonstrates architectural understanding here.

questions.title: Middleware vs. Point-to-Point Integration Architecture
questions.prompt: A company currently has six separate point-to-point integrations connecting Salesforce to six different systems (ERP, marketing automation, billing, a data warehouse, a support ticketing tool, and an identity provider). As the architect, do you recommend introducing a middleware/integration platform layer, and how do you justify that decision?
questions.modelAnswer: Six point-to-point integrations create a combinatorial maintenance problem: each integration has its own authentication setup, its own error handling and retry logic, its own data transformation code, and its own monitoring, so the total maintenance surface scales roughly with the number of connections rather than the number of systems, and any shared concern (like needing to add a new field to every outbound sync, or standardizing retry behavior) has to be reimplemented six separate times. Introducing a middleware layer (an iPaaS like MuleSoft, Boomi, or a similar platform) converts this into a hub-and-spoke model where each system integrates once with the middleware rather than with every other system it needs to talk to, centralizing authentication management, transformation logic, error handling/retry/alerting, and monitoring in one place that's maintained once — the real justification is this maintenance-surface reduction and the operational visibility it provides, not just 'middleware is best practice.' The case against introducing middleware, which an architect should genuinely weigh rather than assume away, is the added cost (licensing, a new skill set the team needs, and the middleware platform itself becoming a new single point of failure and a new system to govern) — for an org with only two or three simple, stable integrations, middleware is often unjustified overhead, and point-to-point remains the right call when the integration count is low and unlikely to grow. At six integrations spanning this many different systems with presumably different data needs (ERP, billing, and a data warehouse in particular likely all need overlapping customer/order data), the maintenance-surface argument is strong enough to justify the migration, but it should be executed incrementally — route new integrations through the middleware first, then migrate existing point-to-point integrations one at a time starting with the ones causing the most current operational pain, rather than attempting a risky simultaneous cutover of all six.
questions.professionalAnswer: My honest answer is yes, but I'd make sure I'm justifying it for the right reason, not just 'middleware is best practice.' Six point-to-point integrations means six separate sets of authentication, error handling, retry logic, and monitoring — if I need to change something that affects every outbound sync, I'm doing that work six times instead of once. Middleware turns that into hub-and-spoke: every system talks to the integration platform once, and things like auth, transformation, and retry logic live in one place I maintain once instead of six times. I would genuinely weigh the other side, though — middleware isn't free, it's a new licensing cost, a new skill the team needs, and a new system that itself becomes a single point of failure you now have to govern. For two or three simple integrations that aren't growing, I'd actually tell a client to skip it. But at six integrations across systems that clearly share overlapping data needs — ERP, billing, and the warehouse are all probably touching customer and order data — the maintenance case is strong enough here. I wouldn't do a risky big-bang cutover of all six at once, though — I'd route any new integration through the middleware first, then migrate the existing ones one at a time, starting with whichever one is causing the most operational pain right now.

questions.title: SAML vs. OAuth 2.0: Designing Identity Architecture for SSO and API Access
questions.prompt: An enterprise customer needs both single sign-on into Salesforce for their employees and a separate API integration where an external service needs to call Salesforce on its own behalf, unattended. Design the identity architecture, explaining why SAML and OAuth 2.0 are not interchangeable here.
questions.modelAnswer: SAML is a protocol for browser-based, user-present authentication: an identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, etc.) asserts a user's identity to Salesforce via a signed XML assertion exchanged through browser redirects, which is exactly the right fit for employees logging into Salesforce through a browser session, and Salesforce supports this via a SAML SSO configuration where the IdP is the source of truth for authentication while Salesforce still manages authorization (profiles, permission sets) locally. OAuth 2.0 is fundamentally different in purpose: it's an authorization framework for granting a client application scoped access to a resource on a user's behalf (or, in the client credentials flow, on behalf of the application itself with no user present at all), which is exactly what's needed for the unattended external service calling Salesforce's API — a Connected App configured for the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials flow, authenticating via a Named Credential/External Credential pair, issues the service a scoped access token without any browser redirect or human login step. The architectural mistake to avoid is trying to use SAML for the machine-to-machine API scenario (SAML has no clean mechanism for unattended, user-absent authentication designed for recurring automated calls) or trying to use OAuth's interactive authorization-code flow for the employee SSO scenario (it would technically work but duplicates what SAML already does better for browser-based enterprise SSO, and most enterprise IdPs standardize on SAML or OIDC for workforce SSO specifically). The correct combined architecture uses SAML (or OIDC, OAuth's modern authentication-focused sibling, if the IdP prefers it) for employee SSO into the Salesforce UI, and a separate OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials-based Connected App plus Named Credential for the unattended service integration — these are two different identity problems solved by two different, purpose-built mechanisms, not one protocol doing double duty.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by making sure the client understands these solve two genuinely different problems, because I see people try to force one protocol to do both jobs. SAML is built for browser-based, user-present login — an identity provider vouches for who the person is via a signed assertion during a browser redirect, which is exactly the employee SSO case. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework, not primarily an authentication one, and its Client Credentials flow specifically is built for exactly this unattended, no-human-involved service-to-service case — a Connected App issues the external service a scoped access token with no browser, no login screen, nothing interactive at all. Trying to use SAML for that machine-to-machine case doesn't really work, because SAML has no clean story for unattended recurring automated calls. And trying to use OAuth's interactive flow for employee SSO is technically possible but it's reinventing something SAML already does better for enterprise workforce login, and most identity providers are built around SAML or OIDC for exactly that use case. So the architecture I'd actually hand them is SAML for employee SSO into the UI, and a separate OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials Connected App with a Named Credential for the unattended integration — two different identity problems, two purpose-built mechanisms, not one protocol stretched to cover both.

questions.title: Shield Platform Encryption: Deterministic vs. Probabilistic Encryption Schemes
questions.prompt: A healthcare company needs to encrypt several PII fields at rest using Shield Platform Encryption, but also needs to run exact-match filters and some reporting against those fields. Design the encryption scheme choices and explain the real tradeoffs.
questions.modelAnswer: Shield Platform Encryption offers probabilistic encryption as the default scheme, where the same plaintext value encrypts to a different ciphertext each time, which provides the strongest protection against pattern analysis but means the field can't be used in a WHERE clause filter, a lookup, or most standard reports, since the database can no longer compare ciphertext values for equality. Deterministic encryption produces the same ciphertext for the same plaintext every time, which makes exact-match filtering, external ID lookups, and certain report filters work correctly against the encrypted field, but at a real security cost: because identical values produce identical ciphertext, an attacker with access to the raw encrypted data (and some auxiliary information, like knowing the distribution of values) can in principle infer patterns or confirm guesses about specific records' values through frequency analysis — it's still far better than plaintext, but it's a deliberately weaker guarantee than probabilistic encryption, which is why Salesforce requires explicitly opting into deterministic encryption per field rather than defaulting to it. The architectural decision is therefore field-by-field: fields that only need protection at rest with no requirement for filtering or exact-match lookup should use probabilistic encryption as the stronger default, while only the specific fields that genuinely need exact-match filtering (for example, a national ID number used as an external key for lookups, or a field a report must filter on) should be explicitly configured for deterministic encryption, accepting that narrower, documented tradeoff only where the business requirement actually demands it. For reporting broadly, it's worth noting that even deterministic encryption doesn't restore full reporting capability (range filters, sorting, and aggregate functions on encrypted fields remain unsupported regardless of scheme), so the architecture should also identify which reports genuinely need to operate on these PII fields and consider whether some of that reporting need is better served by a redacted/masked or tokenized representation surfaced outside the encrypted field entirely, rather than trying to force every reporting need through the encryption scheme choice.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this field by field, not as one blanket decision. Probabilistic encryption is the stronger default — same value encrypts differently every time, which is great for protection but means you can't filter or exact-match on it at all, because the database can't compare ciphertext for equality anymore. Deterministic encryption is the one that lets exact-match filtering and lookups actually work, because the same plaintext always produces the same ciphertext — but that's also exactly why it's weaker: identical ciphertext for identical values means someone with the raw encrypted data and some outside knowledge could potentially do frequency analysis and infer things about specific records. It's still way better than plaintext, but it's a real, narrower tradeoff, which is why Salesforce makes you explicitly opt into it per field rather than just defaulting to it. So my actual recommendation is: default to probabilistic everywhere, and only flip specific fields to deterministic where there's a genuine, named business need — like a national ID being used as a lookup key. And I'd flag to the team up front that even deterministic encryption doesn't give you back range filters, sorting, or aggregates on that field — so for some of this PII reporting need, a tokenized or masked field surfaced separately might actually serve the business better than trying to force every report through the encryption scheme itself.
commonMistakes: Defaults every PII field to deterministic encryption to enable filtering everywhere, ignoring the security tradeoff
Doesn't explain the real security weakness of deterministic encryption (frequency/pattern analysis risk)
Assumes deterministic encryption restores full reporting capability (range filters, sorting, aggregates)
Treats the encryption scheme choice as a single org-wide decision instead of field-by-field
keyPoints: Correctly explains probabilistic encryption as the stronger, filter-incompatible default
Correctly explains deterministic encryption's exact-match capability and its real security weakness
Makes the decision field-by-field based on genuine filtering/lookup need
Notes deterministic encryption still doesn't restore full reporting (range/sort/aggregate) capability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains probabilistic encryption and its limitations
Correctly explains deterministic encryption's capability and real security tradeoff
Makes a correct field-by-field recommendation
Correctly notes the remaining reporting limitations even with deterministic encryption

questions.title: Designing a Salesforce DX Branching Strategy and CI/CD Pipeline
questions.prompt: Design a branching strategy and CI/CD pipeline for a team of three scrum teams using Salesforce DX with scratch orgs, source-driven development, and 2GP unlocked packages, covering how a feature moves from a scratch org to production.
questions.modelAnswer: A workable branching strategy uses a long-lived main/trunk branch that always reflects what's actually in production, short-lived feature branches cut from main for each story (one feature branch per developer per story, not per team), and environment-aligned integration branches (or, in a trunk-based variant, no integration branches at all and instead frequent small merges to main gated entirely by CI) — the key architectural decision is trunk-based development with short-lived branches over long-lived team or release branches, because long-lived branches reintroduce exactly the merge-conflict and drift problems the DX/packaging investment was meant to solve. The pipeline itself: on feature-branch push, CI spins up a fresh scratch org from the project's scratch org definition file, pushes source, runs Apex tests and any Jest/LWC unit tests, and reports pass/fail on the pull request before a human reviews it; on merge to main, CI builds and validates the relevant 2GP unlocked package version(s) against a fresh scratch org, then promotes that validated package version through a sequence of environments — a QA/staging sandbox first, then a UAT sandbox, then production — using the same package version artifact at every stage rather than rebuilding from source at each environment, which is the core promise of package-based release: you test the exact artifact, not a close approximation of it, at every step. Approval gates between environments (a release manager or the architecture review board approving promotion from UAT to production) should be enforced in the pipeline tool itself (manual approval steps in the CI/CD platform) rather than relying on a Slack message or a calendar invite, since an unenforced human gate is the step most likely to get skipped under deadline pressure. The three-team structure maps naturally onto one package per team's domain, each with its own CI pipeline validating independently, with a final integration stage that validates all three packages' current versions together against a shared staging sandbox before the combined promotion to production, catching cross-package interaction issues that each team's isolated pipeline wouldn't surface alone.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push hard for trunk-based development here — a main branch that always reflects production, short feature branches per story, and frequent small merges — because long-lived team or release branches are exactly what reintroduces the merge pain this whole DX investment was supposed to fix. On the pipeline side: every feature branch push spins up a fresh scratch org, pushes source, runs the Apex and LWC tests, and reports back on the pull request before any human even looks at it. Once something merges to main, CI builds an actual versioned 2GP package and validates that specific version against a clean scratch org — and here's the part I really care about: that exact package version is what gets promoted through QA, then UAT, then production, not rebuilt fresh at each stage. That's the whole point of package-based release — you're testing the actual artifact at every step, not a close approximation of it. I'd also insist the approval gates between environments live inside the CI/CD tool itself as real manual-approval steps, not a Slack message somebody's supposed to remember to send, because an unenforced human gate is exactly the step that gets skipped when a deadline's tight. And for the three-team structure, I'd give each team their own package aligned to their domain with its own independent pipeline, plus one final integration stage that validates all three packages together in a shared staging sandbox before the combined production promotion — that's what catches the cross-package issues no single team's pipeline would ever see on its own.
commonMistakes: Proposes long-lived team or release branches instead of trunk-based short-lived branches
Rebuilds from source at each environment instead of promoting the same validated package artifact
Relies on an informal/manual notification for environment promotion approval instead of an enforced CI gate
Doesn't design a final cross-team integration validation stage, missing cross-package interaction issues
keyPoints: Recommends trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches
Designs a CI pipeline that validates against fresh scratch orgs per feature branch
Promotes the same validated package artifact through environments rather than rebuilding
Enforces approval gates in the CI/CD tool and adds a cross-team integration validation stage

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recommends and justifies trunk-based development
Designs a correct CI validation pipeline using scratch orgs
Correctly designs artifact-based promotion through environments
Designs enforced approval gates and cross-team integration validation

questions.title: Environment Strategy: Sandbox Types and Promotion Path for a Large Org
questions.prompt: Design a sandbox/environment strategy for a large org with three development teams, a dedicated QA function, and strict change-control requirements, explaining which sandbox types to use where and why.
questions.modelAnswer: The strategy should use Developer or Developer Pro sandboxes (or, increasingly, scratch orgs for most day-to-day feature work if the org has adopted source-driven development) as the individual development tier, refreshed frequently and cheaply since they don't need production data volume; a shared Partial Copy sandbox (or dedicated Partial Copy sandboxes per team if contention is a problem) as the integration/QA tier, which includes a representative sample of production data and metadata, giving QA a realistic-enough dataset to test against without the cost and refresh time of a Full sandbox; a Full sandbox as the UAT/staging tier, refreshed on a deliberate cadence (commonly aligned to major release cycles) since it carries complete production data and metadata and is the closest pre-production approximation to how a change will actually behave, including realistic data volume for performance-sensitive testing; and production itself as the final tier, reached only through the governed promotion path. The promotion path itself should be strictly directional — change moves from development through QA/Partial Copy through UAT/Full sandbox and finally to production — with each stage gated by passing automated tests plus an explicit sign-off appropriate to that stage (a QA lead's sign-off before promotion to UAT, a change advisory board or release manager's sign-off before promotion to production), and critically, Full sandbox refresh cadence needs to be planned and communicated because a refresh wipes any in-flight UAT configuration changes that weren't captured in source control, which is a common and painful surprise if refresh timing isn't coordinated with release timing. For strict change control specifically, every promotion step should be traceable to a specific package version or change set and a specific approval record, not just 'someone deployed it,' and the environment strategy document itself should be treated as a living architecture artifact reviewed whenever the org's scale or team structure changes meaningfully, rather than a one-time setup decision.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lay this out as four real tiers. Individual dev work happens in Developer or Developer Pro sandboxes — or scratch orgs if the team's gone source-driven — cheap to refresh, no need for real data volume there. QA gets a Partial Copy sandbox, maybe one per team if they're stepping on each other, because that gives a realistic slice of production data without the cost and refresh time of a full copy. UAT and staging live in a Full sandbox, refreshed on a deliberate cadence tied to the release calendar, because that's the closest thing to production you've got — real data volume, real metadata, genuinely useful for performance-sensitive testing. And production is the final stop, reached only through the governed path. The promotion itself needs to be strictly one direction — dev, then QA, then UAT, then production — with a real sign-off at each gate, not just a Slack thumbs-up. The thing I always warn teams about explicitly is Full sandbox refresh timing — a refresh wipes any UAT configuration that wasn't captured in source control, and I've seen that catch teams completely off guard when a refresh lands in the middle of a UAT cycle nobody coordinated with the release calendar. And for strict change control, I want every single promotion traceable to an actual package version and an actual approval record — 'someone deployed it' isn't good enough once you've got this many teams and this much scrutiny.
commonMistakes: Uses Full sandboxes for individual developer work, wasting cost and refresh time unnecessarily
Doesn't account for Full sandbox refresh wiping uncaptured UAT configuration
No explicit sign-off/approval gate between environment tiers
Doesn't make promotions traceable to specific package versions/change sets for audit purposes
keyPoints: Correctly assigns sandbox types (Developer/scratch, Partial Copy, Full) to the right tier
Designs a strictly directional, gated promotion path
Flags Full sandbox refresh cadence and its risk to in-flight UAT configuration
Requires traceable promotion records for strict change control

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns the right sandbox type to each environment tier
Designs a correct, gated, directional promotion path
Flags the Full sandbox refresh/UAT coordination risk
Addresses traceability requirements for strict change control

questions.title: Event-Driven Architecture Across Clouds Using Platform Events
questions.prompt: A company runs Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, and a custom-built order management system outside Salesforce. Design an event-driven architecture so that a case escalation in Service Cloud automatically triggers a priority review workflow in the external order management system and updates a related Opportunity in Sales Cloud, without tight coupling between the three systems.
questions.modelAnswer: The core design principle is that the Case-escalation Apex/Flow logic publishes a single custom Platform Event (e.g., CaseEscalated__e) describing the business fact that occurred, with a payload carrying the relevant IDs and context, rather than the escalation logic directly calling out to the order management system or directly updating the Opportunity — this decouples the publisher from needing to know anything about its consumers, so adding a third or fourth consumer later requires zero changes to the escalation logic itself. The external order management system subscribes to this Platform Event via the Pub/Sub API (using a gRPC client library in whatever language the system is built in) and runs its own priority-review workflow independently when it receives the event, meaning the order management system's internal logic and the Salesforce escalation logic never need to know about each other's implementation details, only the agreed event schema. The Opportunity update is handled by a second, independent subscriber — either an Apex trigger on a Platform Event-triggered flow, or another Apex class implementing the event trigger pattern — that listens to the same CaseEscalated__e event and updates the related Opportunity, running in parallel with (and completely independent of) the external system's subscription, so a slowdown or outage in the external order management system's processing has zero effect on the Opportunity update happening inside Salesforce. This architecture's resilience comes from Platform Events' durable, replayable delivery (a subscriber that's briefly down can replay from where it left off within the retention window) rather than requiring the publisher to guarantee synchronous delivery to every consumer, and the architecture should define the event schema itself as a versioned contract (documented, with a deprecation policy for fields) since multiple independent consumers now depend on it and a breaking payload change would affect all of them simultaneously.
questions.professionalAnswer: The design principle I'd lead with is: the case escalation logic should publish one event describing what happened, and have zero knowledge of who's listening or what they do with it. So when a case escalates, Apex or Flow publishes a CaseEscalated event with the relevant IDs and context — it doesn't call the external order system directly, and it doesn't update the Opportunity directly either. The external order management system subscribes to that event over Pub/Sub API using its own gRPC client and runs its priority-review workflow completely independently — it never needs to know anything about Salesforce's internal escalation logic, just the event's shape. The Opportunity update is a second, separate subscriber to that exact same event, running inside Salesforce independently of whatever the external system is doing — so if that external system is slow or temporarily down, that has zero effect on the Opportunity getting updated. The resilience here comes from Platform Events being durable and replayable — a subscriber that's briefly offline can catch up within the retention window instead of just losing events. And because multiple systems now depend on this event's shape, I'd treat the event schema itself as a real versioned contract, documented, with a deprecation policy — because a careless field change would break every consumer depending on it at once, not just one.
commonMistakes: Has the escalation logic call out directly to the external system and/or update the Opportunity synchronously, creating tight coupling
Designs only one consumer instead of two independent subscribers to the same event
Doesn't leverage Platform Events' replay/durability, assuming synchronous delivery guarantees instead
Doesn't treat the event payload schema as a versioned contract with multiple dependents
keyPoints: Publishes a single decoupled business event rather than calling consumers directly
Designs independent subscribers for the external system and the Opportunity update
Leverages Platform Events' durability/replay for resilience instead of synchronous guarantees
Treats the event schema as a versioned contract given multiple dependents

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs a decoupled publish/subscribe architecture
Correctly designs independent, parallel subscribers for both consumers
Correctly leverages Platform Events' durability/replay for resilience
Treats the event schema as a versioned contract

questions.title: Designing an Enterprise Architecture for Merging Two Salesforce Orgs Post-Acquisition
questions.prompt: Your company acquired a competitor that runs its own separate Salesforce org. Leadership wants the two orgs merged within 12 months. Design the high-level enterprise application architecture for this merger, including how you'd sequence it.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture starts with choosing a direction (merge the acquired org into the acquirer's org, or vice versa, or in rare cases build a new target org) based on which org's object model, customizations, and integration ecosystem is the better foundation to extend, rather than defaulting to 'the bigger company's org wins' — a smaller org with cleaner architecture is sometimes the better target even if counterintuitive politically. Once direction is set, the sequence should be: first, a data model reconciliation phase mapping every object, field, and automation in the source org against the target org's equivalent (or lack thereof), explicitly cataloging true duplicates, fields that need new homes, and business processes that differ enough to require a record-type-based reconciliation rather than a straight field mapping; second, an integration and dependency audit of every external system connected to the source org (its own ERP connection, marketing tools, support tools) to determine which need to be re-pointed at the target org, decommissioned, or run in parallel temporarily; third, a phased data migration (not big-bang) that moves master data (Accounts, Contacts) first with careful deduplication against the target org's existing records using an MDM-style matching process, then transactional data (Opportunities, Cases) using the now-resolved external-ID mappings from the master data migration; and finally, user migration and training, cutting users over from the source org to the target org in waves aligned with the data migration waves rather than all at once. Given a 12-month timeline, the biggest architectural risk is treating this as a lift-and-shift exercise under deadline pressure, importing the source org's processes wholesale into the target org to save time, which recreates both orgs' worst inconsistencies in one newly merged org rather than achieving the simplification the merger was supposed to deliver — the honest architectural recommendation to leadership should include naming this risk explicitly and proposing a prioritized reconciliation (the highest-value, most-used processes get real reconciliation effort; lower-value edge-case processes get a pragmatic, faster resolution) given the fixed timeline, rather than promising full reconciliation of everything in 12 months without naming what gets deprioritized.
questions.professionalAnswer: First decision I'd actually push leadership to make deliberately, not by default, is which org is the target — it's not automatically 'the acquirer's org wins,' sometimes the smaller acquired org has the cleaner architecture and is the better foundation to build on, even if that's a harder political conversation. Once that's settled, I'd sequence this as: reconcile the data models first — every object and field in the source org mapped against the target, flagging true duplicates versus things that need a genuinely different home versus processes different enough to need record types instead of a simple field mapping. Then audit every external integration hanging off the source org, because those all need a decision — re-point at the target org, decommission, or run in parallel for a while. Then migrate data in phases, not big-bang — master data first, with real deduplication against what's already in the target org, then transactional data once those master records have stable external IDs to resolve against. Users move over in waves aligned with the data migration, not all at once on day one. And honestly, the biggest risk I'd name to leadership up front on a 12-month timeline is the temptation to just lift-and-shift the source org's processes wholesale to hit the deadline — that doesn't actually merge anything, it just recreates both orgs' mess inside one org. I'd rather tell them now which processes get real reconciliation effort and which get a faster, more pragmatic resolution, than quietly let that tradeoff happen by accident under deadline pressure.
commonMistakes: Assumes the acquirer's org is automatically the merge target without evaluating architecture quality
Proposes a big-bang data migration instead of phased master-data-first migration
Doesn't audit external integrations hanging off the source org before migration
Doesn't name the lift-and-shift risk of the fixed timeline, promising full reconciliation without naming tradeoffs
keyPoints: Deliberately chooses the merge direction/target rather than defaulting to the acquirer's org
Sequences data model reconciliation before data migration
Audits and plans for external integrations connected to the source org
Names the lift-and-shift risk given the fixed timeline and proposes prioritized reconciliation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Deliberately evaluates and chooses the merge direction/target
Correctly sequences reconciliation, integration audit, and phased data migration
Addresses external integration dependencies on the source org
Names the timeline/lift-and-shift risk and proposes a prioritized approach

questions.title: LDV and Sharing Architecture Design for a 200-Million-Record Org
questions.prompt: Design the data and sharing architecture for a custom 'Service_Event__c' object expected to grow to 200 million records over three years, used by field service reps who need to see only events for accounts in their territory, with reporting requirements for regional managers. Walk through your full design.
questions.modelAnswer: The design starts from the access pattern, not the schema: field reps need territory-scoped record-level access, which at 200 million records makes criteria-based or owner-based sharing rules alone prohibitively expensive to recalculate at every territory or ownership change, so the design should use Enterprise Territory Management's rule-based account assignment (reps assigned to territories, territories resolve account membership by rule) combined with the standard territory-based sharing that flows from account access down to related records like Service_Event__c, rather than hand-built sharing rules on the object itself — this keeps sharing recalculation scoped to territory/account changes rather than every individual event record. For query performance at this scale, Service_Event__c needs a skinny table requested from Salesforce covering the handful of fields reps and reports actually filter on (status, territory-derived field, event date), and all SOQL/report filters need to be audited for selectivity against indexed fields, with a particular eye on date-range filters, which are common in field-service reporting and need an indexed date field rather than a formula-derived date to stay selective. Regional manager reporting at this volume likely exceeds what standard Salesforce reports can perform well against even with a skinny table, so the design should route manager-facing aggregate reporting through CRM Analytics (which handles large-dataset aggregation more efficiently than standard reports) or, if cross-system reporting is also needed, through a modern-data-stack path where Service_Event__c data is extracted via Bulk API into a warehouse for the heaviest aggregate reporting, with Salesforce itself reserved for operational, record-level access. Finally, given the three-year growth trajectory, the design needs an explicit data retention/archival policy from day one — deciding now whether events older than some threshold get archived out of Salesforce entirely (to a warehouse, keeping Salesforce's live working set smaller) rather than waiting until the object is already at 200 million rows to discover that unbounded retention was never actually a requirement, which is the single highest-leverage LDV decision available and the easiest one to get wrong by not deciding it explicitly up front.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start from the access pattern, not the object's fields. Reps need territory-scoped access, and at 200 million records, I'm not going to lean on criteria-based sharing rules that need heavy recalculation every time someone's territory changes — I'd use Enterprise Territory Management so reps are assigned to territories and territory-based sharing flows down to these event records, which keeps recalculation scoped to territory and account changes instead of touching every individual record. For performance, I'd request a skinny table from Salesforce covering just the handful of fields reps and reports actually filter on, and I'd go audit every existing SOQL and report filter for real selectivity — date-range filters are the thing I'd check hardest, because field service reporting leans on those constantly, and they need to hit an indexed date field, not something formula-derived. For the regional manager reporting, honestly, at 200 million rows I don't think standard Salesforce reports are the right tool even with a skinny table — I'd push that to CRM Analytics, or if there's a real cross-system reporting need, extract this data via Bulk API into a warehouse and let Salesforce stay focused on operational, record-level access for the reps. And the thing I'd insist on deciding now, not two years from now: a retention and archival policy. Deciding today whether events older than some threshold get archived out of Salesforce is the single highest-leverage call on this whole design, and it's exactly the kind of decision that gets made by default — meaning nobody decides, and you end up with 200 million rows of data nobody actually needed to keep live.
commonMistakes: Designs hand-built sharing rules on the object instead of leveraging territory-based sharing at this scale
Doesn't request a skinny table or audit query selectivity for a 200-million-row object
Assumes standard Salesforce reports will perform adequately at this volume for manager reporting
Doesn't address data retention/archival, leaving unbounded growth undecided
keyPoints: Designs territory-based sharing rather than hand-built sharing rules at this scale
Requests a skinny table and audits query selectivity
Routes heavy aggregate reporting to CRM Analytics or an external warehouse rather than standard reports
Establishes an explicit data retention/archival policy given the growth trajectory

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs territory-based sharing appropriate for this scale
Correctly addresses LDV query/report performance (skinny table, selectivity)
Correctly routes heavy reporting away from standard reports at this scale
Establishes an explicit retention/archival policy

deepDive.heading: Start from the access pattern, not the schema
deepDive.content: At 200 million records, the sharing design has to be decided before worrying about fields or page layouts, because sharing recalculation cost is driven by model complexity and record volume together. The access requirement — reps see only events for accounts in their territory — maps cleanly onto Enterprise Territory Management rather than hand-built criteria-based sharing rules, because territory membership changes (a rep's territory assignment, a territory's rule-based account resolution) are relatively infrequent compared to the record volume, and territory-based sharing's recalculation scope is tied to account/territory changes, not to the 200 million child Service_Event__c records individually.

deepDive.heading: Object and sharing model design
deepDive.content: Service_Event__c should inherit access via its master-detail or lookup relationship to Account (or via Apex-managed sharing keyed off the related Account's territory, if master-detail isn't appropriate for other reasons like needing independent ownership). Avoid object-level criteria-based sharing rules entirely at this volume — they require full-object recalculation on rule or criteria changes, which at 200 million rows is exactly the expensive operation the earlier troubleshooting scenario in this bank describes taking hours. Territory-based inherited sharing keeps the recalculation surface proportional to account/territory changes, not event-record volume.

deepDive.heading: Query and storage performance
deepDive.content: Request a skinny table covering the fields reps filter on operationally (status, territory/account reference, event date) and the fields managers' reports filter on, keeping it under the practical column ceiling by excluding rarely-filtered fields. Audit every SOQL query and report filter for genuine selectivity against indexed fields — with explicit attention to date-range filters, which are common in field-service use cases and need to filter on an actual indexed date field, not a formula field, to remain selective. Consider a custom index on any non-standard field that's filtered on frequently but isn't naturally indexed.

deepDive.heading: Reporting architecture for regional managers
deepDive.content: Standard Salesforce reports, even against a skinny table, typically can't aggregate cleanly across tens or hundreds of millions of rows with the responsiveness managers expect. Route manager-facing aggregate reporting to CRM Analytics, which is built for exactly this kind of large-dataset aggregation, or, if the reporting need extends beyond Salesforce data (blending with other systems), extract Service_Event__c via Bulk API into a warehouse (e.g., Snowflake) and build the aggregate reporting there with dbt-modeled rollups, keeping Salesforce itself focused on the operational, record-level access reps actually need day to day.

deepDive.heading: Data retention and archival policy
deepDive.content: This is the single highest-leverage decision in the whole design and the easiest one to skip. Growth to 200 million records over three years is itself a choice, not a given — deciding now whether events older than some business-defined threshold (e.g., 18 months) get archived out of Salesforce into a warehouse, with only recent/active events staying live in Salesforce, keeps the live working set's growth bounded and keeps every downstream performance decision (skinny table, sharing recalculation, storage cost) proportional to a manageable number rather than an ever-growing one. Deciding this after the object has already reached 200 million rows means re-architecting under much worse conditions than deciding it at design time.

deepDive.heading: Sequencing and validation
deepDive.content: This design should be validated with a representative data volume test well before production scale is reached — load a realistic multi-million-row test dataset into a Full sandbox and measure actual sharing recalculation time, report performance, and query plan behavior rather than assuming the design will hold at scale based on theory alone. Any assumption that doesn't hold under real LDV testing needs to be caught during the design phase, not discovered during year two of production growth.

questions.title: Big Bang vs. Phased Data Migration Strategy
questions.prompt: A company is migrating 15 years of customer data from a legacy CRM into Salesforce. Compare a big-bang cutover migration against a phased migration strategy, and recommend one for this scenario with justification.
questions.modelAnswer: A big-bang migration moves all data in a single cutover event, typically over a weekend or defined freeze window, with the legacy system retired (or made read-only) immediately after — its advantage is simplicity of the end state (no dual-maintenance period, no synchronization between old and new systems to manage) and a single, bounded period of business risk rather than an extended one, but its disadvantage is that the entire 15 years of data quality, transformation, and validation work has to be correct before that single cutover, with no opportunity to validate against real production usage before the full volume and full user base depends on it, and any significant defect discovered post-cutover is now a production incident rather than a controlled pre-migration fix. A phased migration moves data and/or user groups in waves — by business unit, by data type (master data before transactional data, or recent data before historical archive data), or by a combination — which reduces risk per wave and allows lessons from early waves (transformation bugs, unexpected data quality issects) to improve later waves, but requires maintaining some form of synchronization or dual-system operation during the transition period, which is itself nontrivial engineering and a real source of its own risk (data drift between systems, users confused about which system is authoritative for what). For 15 years of legacy customer data specifically, a phased approach is the stronger recommendation: data quality issues accumulated over 15 years are close to certain to include edge cases that won't surface until migration is actually attempted, and discovering those in a first wave covering, for instance, the most recent two years of active customers (lower volume, higher data quality, immediately validatable against business users who can confirm correctness) is far lower-risk than discovering them for the first time during a single irreversible cutover covering the full 15-year history. The specific phasing recommendation is: migrate master data (Accounts, Contacts) first across the full historical range since that's needed as the foundation regardless of phasing, then migrate transactional/activity data in waves ordered by recency (most recent and most actively used data first, since that's what users interact with daily and where correctness matters most immediately), with older historical/archival data migrated last and potentially to a lower-touch destination (e.g., a linked archive rather than fully active records) if the business confirms it doesn't need full day-to-day Salesforce functionality against 15-year-old records.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recommend phased here, and I'd be specific about why. Big bang's appeal is a clean end state — no juggling two systems, one bounded weekend of risk instead of a long drawn-out one — but it means every bit of transformation and data-quality work across fifteen years of legacy data has to be right before that one cutover, with zero chance to validate against real usage first. And fifteen years of accumulated legacy data is essentially guaranteed to have edge cases nobody's going to find until someone actually tries to migrate it — finding those during a single irreversible cutover is a production incident, not a fixable mistake. Phased migration costs you something real too — you're maintaining some kind of sync or dual-system operation during the transition, which is its own engineering risk, data can drift between the two systems if you're not careful. But for this specific case, I'd still go phased: start with master data across the full history since you need that foundation regardless, then migrate transactional data in waves starting with the most recent, most actively-used stuff first — that's lower volume, probably better data quality, and it's what users are touching every day, so you get real validation fast. Older historical data goes last, and honestly I'd ask the business whether fifteen-year-old records genuinely need full day-to-day Salesforce functionality or whether a lighter-touch archive destination actually serves them just as well.
commonMistakes: Recommends big-bang for a large, historically messy dataset without acknowledging the validation risk
Doesn't name the real cost of phased migration (dual-system sync/maintenance during transition)
Doesn't propose a concrete phasing order (master data, then recency-ordered transactional data)
Doesn't question whether old historical data needs the same migration treatment as active data
keyPoints: Correctly explains big-bang's risk/simplicity tradeoff
Correctly explains phased migration's risk-reduction benefit and its own dual-system cost
Recommends phased migration with sound justification for this scenario
Proposes a concrete, sensible phasing order (master data, then recency-ordered transactional data)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the tradeoffs of both strategies
Makes and justifies a clear recommendation for this scenario
Proposes a concrete, sensible phasing order
Addresses the real cost/risk of the recommended approach honestly

questions.title: Data Modeling for a Multi-Org, Multi-System Landscape
questions.prompt: A company has customer data living in Salesforce, an ERP, and a marketing platform, each with its own notion of 'customer' and its own identifier. Design a data model and system-of-record strategy that lets these three systems interoperate without forcing one platform to own every attribute.
questions.modelAnswer: The correct model rejects the idea of one platform owning the entire customer record and instead assigns system-of-record status per attribute domain: Salesforce is authoritative for sales/relationship attributes (account ownership, opportunity history, support case history), the ERP is authoritative for financial/transactional attributes (billing terms, invoice history, credit status), and the marketing platform is authoritative for engagement attributes (campaign history, email preferences, lead scoring) — no single system should be forced to be the master of data it doesn't actually originate or primarily act on. Interoperability requires a cross-system identity resolution layer: either a dedicated MDM tool or a warehouse-based matching process (deterministic matching on a shared identifier where one exists, like a tax ID or email, supplemented by probabilistic matching — fuzzy name/address matching — where it doesn't) that establishes and maintains a canonical customer ID mapped to each system's local identifier, published back to each system (often via reverse ETL) so each system can store the canonical ID as a cross-reference field without needing to become the source of truth for the others' data. Each system's data model should store only its own authoritative attributes plus the canonical cross-reference ID, pulling other systems' attributes on demand (via a live callout, a cached sync, or a unified reporting layer) rather than duplicating and attempting to keep every attribute in sync across all three systems, which both reduces data staleness risk and makes clear, for any given attribute, exactly one place a user or integration should go to get or change the authoritative value. The governance requirement this model creates is a documented attribute-ownership map (a simple table: attribute, system of record, sync direction, update frequency) reviewed by an architecture or data governance board whenever a new system joins the landscape or a new attribute is introduced, since without that explicit map, duplicated and drifting attribute definitions re-emerge exactly the way they did before this design was introduced.
questions.professionalAnswer: The mistake I'd steer this company away from is trying to make one platform own the whole customer record — that's not actually true of any of these three systems today, and forcing it creates more problems than it solves. Instead I'd assign system-of-record status attribute by attribute: Salesforce owns the sales and relationship history, the ERP owns billing and financial attributes, the marketing platform owns engagement and campaign data — each system stays authoritative for what it actually originates. To make that work across systems, I need an identity resolution layer — either a real MDM tool or a warehouse-based matching process — that builds a canonical customer ID by matching on whatever shared identifiers exist, plus fuzzy matching where they don't, and then pushes that canonical ID back into each system as a cross-reference field. Each system then only stores its own attributes plus that canonical ID, and pulls in the others' data on demand rather than trying to duplicate and keep everything in sync everywhere — that's both less fragile and it means for any given attribute, there's exactly one place anyone should go to change it. And none of this holds up without governance — I'd want a simple, living attribute-ownership map that gets reviewed every time a new system or new attribute enters the picture, because without that explicit document, you end up right back where this company started, with three systems quietly disagreeing about what 'customer' even means.
commonMistakes: Tries to make one platform the single master of the entire customer record
Duplicates and attempts to sync every attribute across all systems instead of pulling on demand
Doesn't design an identity resolution/MDM layer to establish a canonical cross-system ID
No governance mechanism (attribute-ownership map) to prevent the problem from recurring
keyPoints: Assigns system-of-record status per attribute domain, not per whole record
Designs a cross-system identity resolution/MDM layer with deterministic plus probabilistic matching
Each system stores only its own attributes plus a canonical cross-reference ID
Establishes governance (attribute-ownership map) to sustain the model as systems change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rejects single-platform ownership in favor of per-attribute system of record
Correctly designs the identity resolution/MDM layer
Designs a sound on-demand/cross-reference data access pattern
Establishes durable governance for the model

questions.title: CRM Analytics Architecture at Scale Across Multiple Business Units
questions.prompt: A company wants to roll out CRM Analytics across five business units, each with its own Salesforce data, some shared security requirements, and a need for some company-wide executive dashboards. Design the app, dataset, and security architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: The architecture should use one CRM Analytics app per business unit for unit-specific dashboards and recipes, each scoped to that unit's relevant data and owned/maintained by that unit's analysts, rather than one monolithic app trying to serve all five units' differing needs, since a shared app becomes a bottleneck for change and a source of accidental cross-unit visibility if not carefully partitioned. Security should be designed using Row-Level Security (RLS) predicates on each shared or unit-specific dataset, mapped to the underlying Salesforce sharing model (often via a security predicate that references the user's Salesforce role, territory, or a custom permission) rather than relying solely on app-level sharing, since app-level sharing controls who can open a dashboard but RLS is what actually controls which rows within a shared dataset a given user can see — this distinction matters most for the company-wide executive dashboards, where executives need appropriately aggregated visibility across all five units' data while individual business-unit analysts should not gain access to other units' row-level detail just because they're both referencing a shared underlying dataset. For the company-wide executive dashboards specifically, the design should use a separate, purpose-built 'Executive' app with its own datasets built via recipes that aggregate/roll up data sourced from each business unit's recipes (a hub pattern: five unit recipes feed one executive-rollup recipe) rather than directly exposing unit-level row-level datasets to the executive app, which both keeps the aggregation logic centralized in one place and avoids needing to replicate RLS logic across every executive-facing asset. Data governance across five business units needs an explicit naming and folder/app organization convention (so a new analyst in unit three can find what's relevant without wading through four other units' assets) and a shared 'common' layer (for genuinely shared dimensions like a company-wide product catalog or fiscal calendar) that's built once and referenced by all five units' recipes rather than each unit rebuilding its own version of data that's actually identical across units.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build this as five separate apps, one per business unit, each scoped to that unit's own data and owned by that unit's own analysts — a single shared app trying to serve all five ends up being a bottleneck for change, and honestly a security risk if it's not perfectly partitioned. Security-wise, I'd lean on Row-Level Security predicates tied to the actual Salesforce sharing model — role, territory, whatever makes sense — because app-level sharing only controls who can open a dashboard, it doesn't control which rows inside a shared dataset someone can actually see, and that distinction is exactly what matters for the executive dashboards. For those, I wouldn't expose unit-level row data directly to an executive app at all — I'd build a separate executive app with its own rollup recipes that aggregate data sourced from each unit's recipes, hub-and-spoke style, so the aggregation logic lives in one place and I'm not trying to replicate RLS rules across a dozen executive-facing assets. And across all five units, I'd push hard for a shared 'common' layer for things that are genuinely identical everywhere — a product catalog, a fiscal calendar — built once, instead of five units each quietly building their own slightly-different version of the same reference data.
commonMistakes: Builds one monolithic app for all five business units instead of unit-scoped apps
Relies on app-level sharing alone instead of Row-Level Security for row-level data protection
Exposes unit-level row data directly to executive dashboards instead of a rollup/hub pattern
Doesn't establish a shared 'common' layer for genuinely shared reference data
keyPoints: Designs unit-scoped apps rather than one monolithic shared app
Correctly distinguishes app-level sharing from Row-Level Security
Designs a hub-and-spoke rollup pattern for executive-level dashboards
Establishes a shared common data layer for genuinely shared reference data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs unit-scoped apps rather than a monolithic app
Correctly designs Row-Level Security distinct from app-level sharing
Correctly designs the executive rollup/hub pattern
Establishes a shared common data layer across units

questions.title: Designing a Data Governance Framework for an Architecture Review Board
questions.prompt: A company has never had a formal data governance process; data quality issues, duplicate fields, and inconsistent field definitions have accumulated for years. As the architect proposing a governance framework to the Architecture Review Board, what does the framework actually need to contain to be more than a document nobody follows?
questions.modelAnswer: A governance framework that actually gets followed needs ownership assigned to specific named roles, not an abstract committee — a data owner per major object/domain (accountable for that object's field definitions and quality) and a data steward role doing the day-to-day enforcement, because 'governance' owned by everyone and no one is exactly how the current accumulated mess happened in the first place. It needs a concrete, lightweight intake process for any new field or object (a short request form routed to the relevant data owner, checking first whether an existing field already covers the need before approving a new one) enforced as an actual gate — ideally a required approval step in the deployment pipeline itself, not a wiki page people are supposed to remember to check — since a governance rule with no enforcement mechanism is a suggestion, not a framework. It needs defined, measurable data quality standards per critical field (e.g., a required format, a maximum allowable duplicate rate, a mandatory review cadence) with an actual recurring measurement process (a scheduled report or dashboard showing current compliance against those standards) rather than a one-time cleanup effort that quietly decays back to the prior state once the initial project ends, because data governance that isn't continuously measured is governance that silently stops happening within a year. Finally, it needs the Architecture Review Board itself to hold a standing agenda item reviewing governance metrics and any significant proposed new fields/objects at a regular cadence, which is what actually keeps the framework alive rather than letting it become one more initiative that had enthusiasm at launch and no sustained attention six months later — the difference between a framework and a document is precisely this ongoing institutional attention, not the quality of the document's initial content.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the review board plainly: the reason the current mess exists isn't that nobody ever cared about data quality, it's that nothing here was ever actually owned by a specific person, and nothing was ever enforced by anything other than good intentions. So the framework I'd propose starts with real, named ownership — a data owner per major object who's accountable for its field definitions, and stewards doing the actual day-to-day work — not an abstract committee everyone assumes someone else is handling. Then I want a genuinely lightweight intake process for any new field or object, routed to the right data owner, checking first whether something already covers the need — and that has to be an actual gate in the deployment pipeline, not a wiki page people are supposed to remember to check, because an unenforced rule is just a suggestion. I'd also define real, measurable quality standards for the fields that matter most, with a recurring report that actually shows current compliance, because a one-time cleanup always decays back to the same mess within a year if nobody's measuring it continuously. And the thing that actually keeps any of this alive long-term is putting governance metrics on this board's own standing agenda, reviewed regularly — that ongoing attention is the real difference between a framework and a document that gets written once and forgotten.
commonMistakes: Proposes governance owned by an abstract committee instead of named, accountable roles
Designs an intake process with no actual enforcement mechanism in the deployment pipeline
Proposes a one-time data cleanup instead of recurring, measured quality standards
Doesn't give the Architecture Review Board an ongoing, standing role in sustaining the framework
keyPoints: Assigns real, named ownership (data owners, stewards) rather than an abstract committee
Designs an enforced intake gate, not an unenforced suggestion
Defines measurable, recurring data quality standards rather than a one-time cleanup
Gives the Architecture Review Board an ongoing standing role to sustain the framework

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Assigns real, accountable ownership roles
Designs an enforced (not just documented) intake process
Defines measurable, recurring quality standards
Builds in ongoing institutional attention to sustain the framework

questions.title: Designing the Modern Data Stack Alongside Salesforce: Snowflake, dbt, and Reverse ETL
questions.prompt: A retail company wants Salesforce to remain the system of record for customer and order data operationally, but needs a Snowflake-based analytics platform with dbt-governed metrics for cross-system reporting (combining Salesforce with POS and e-commerce data), with some of those computed metrics (like a customer loyalty tier) flowing back into Salesforce for reps to see. Design the full data architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: Salesforce data flows into Snowflake via either Bulk API-based batch extraction (scheduled, for a straightforward nightly refresh need) or Change Data Capture consumed by a CDC-aware ingestion tool (for near-real-time needs), landing in a raw staging layer that mirrors the Salesforce schema with minimal transformation, alongside similarly raw-landed POS and e-commerce data — the architectural principle here is that raw ingestion should never apply business logic, so every downstream consumer works from the same untransformed source of truth regardless of what transformations get built later. dbt then builds the staging-to-intermediate-to-marts layering on top of these raw sources: staging models do only renaming/type-casting per source, intermediate models implement the actual business logic that spans sources (joining Salesforce Order data with POS transaction data and e-commerce order data into one unified 'customer purchase' concept, with the loyalty tier calculation defined exactly once as a dbt model or a dbt Semantic Layer metric), and marts expose the governed, consumption-ready tables for BI tools and for the reverse-ETL sync. The computed loyalty tier, once calculated in dbt's mart layer, is pushed back into Salesforce via a reverse-ETL tool (Hightouch, Census, or similar) that maps the dbt mart's loyalty-tier column to a custom field on the Salesforce Contact or Account object, running on its own schedule appropriate to how frequently loyalty tier genuinely needs to be current (hourly or daily, not necessarily real-time) — and this reverse-ETL mapping should be protected by a dbt model contract on the mart feeding it, so a future column rename or type change fails in CI rather than silently breaking the sync into a production CRM field reps are relying on. The governance discipline this requires is treating the loyalty-tier calculation as owned by exactly one team (data engineering, defining it once in dbt) with Salesforce never recalculating or overriding it locally, and documenting the reverse-ETL-fed field in Salesforce clearly (e.g., a field description noting 'calculated nightly in the data warehouse, not editable') so a future Salesforce admin doesn't add automation that conflicts with a value that's actually owned upstream.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd bring Salesforce data into Snowflake through Bulk API for a straightforward scheduled extract, or CDC if parts of this genuinely need to be near-real-time, landing everything in a raw staging layer that mirrors the source schema with basically zero transformation — same for the POS and e-commerce data. No business logic happens at that raw layer, on purpose, so every downstream consumer is working from the same untouched source. Then dbt does the real work: staging models just rename and type-cast, intermediate models are where the actual cross-system logic lives — joining Salesforce orders with POS and e-commerce transactions into one real 'customer purchase' concept, with the loyalty tier calculated exactly once there, not reinvented anywhere else. That loyalty tier then flows back into Salesforce through a reverse-ETL tool, mapped onto a custom field on the Contact or Account, synced on whatever cadence the business actually needs — probably not real-time, loyalty tier doesn't usually need to be that fresh. The part I'd insist on, because I've seen this break before, is putting a dbt model contract on the mart that feeds that reverse-ETL sync, so a future column rename fails safely in CI instead of silently breaking a field reps are actively relying on in production. And I'd document that Salesforce field explicitly — something like 'calculated nightly upstream, don't build automation on top of this locally' — because the worst version of this architecture is some admin two years from now adding a flow that quietly fights with a value that's actually owned by the data team.
commonMistakes: Applies business logic during raw ingestion instead of keeping staging layers logic-free
Defines the loyalty tier calculation in multiple places instead of exactly once in dbt
Doesn't protect the reverse-ETL-feeding mart with a dbt model contract
Doesn't document the reverse-ETL field in Salesforce, risking future conflicting automation
keyPoints: Correctly designs raw, logic-free ingestion from Salesforce and other sources into Snowflake
Correctly layers dbt staging/intermediate/marts with the loyalty tier defined exactly once
Correctly designs the reverse-ETL sync back into Salesforce with an appropriate cadence
Protects the sync with a model contract and documents the field's upstream ownership in Salesforce

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs raw ingestion into Snowflake from multiple sources
Correctly designs dbt layering with a single-source-of-truth metric definition
Correctly designs the reverse-ETL sync back into Salesforce
Protects the sync with contracts and documentation to prevent future conflicts

questions.title: Territory Management Architecture for a Global Sales Organization
questions.prompt: A global sales organization needs territories defined by a combination of geography, account size tier, and product specialization, with reps sometimes covering multiple overlapping territories. Design the Enterprise Territory Management architecture.
questions.modelAnswer: Enterprise Territory Management supports a territory hierarchy where each territory type and territory can carry its own assignment rules, so the design should model geography as the primary hierarchy backbone (region > sub-region > country, for example) with account-size-tier and product-specialization as either sibling territory dimensions under the relevant geography node or as separate territory models entirely if the business genuinely needs to run size-tier and product-specialization assignment as orthogonal, independently-evolving structures rather than forcing them into one rigid hierarchy. Overlapping coverage (a rep covering multiple territories) is natively supported since Enterprise Territory Management allows a single user to be assigned to multiple territories simultaneously, each potentially with different access/role settings (e.g., a rep might have full edit access in their primary territory but read-only in an overlapping territory they're covering for visibility only) — the architecture should make deliberate, explicit role-per-territory-assignment decisions rather than giving every assignment the same access level by default, since a rep's actual working relationship to an overlapping territory often differs meaningfully from their primary one. Assignment rules should be built to be rule-based and automatically re-resolved (based on account attributes like country, annual revenue tier, or product line) rather than manual, since 15-30% typical annual account attribute changes would otherwise require constant manual territory reassignment at global scale — and the architecture needs a defined process for testing rule changes in a sandbox against a copy of real account data before activating in production, since a territory rule error at this scale can silently misassign access for thousands of accounts simultaneously. Given the complexity of three overlapping dimensions, the design should also include a periodic territory model validation/audit report (orphaned accounts not matching any territory rule, accounts matching multiple territories unexpectedly) run on a schedule, because a model this complex is likely to develop edge-case gaps over time that a reactive 'someone complained they can't see an account' discovery process would surface far too late.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd use geography as the backbone of the territory hierarchy — region, sub-region, country — and then decide deliberately whether size tier and product specialization should live as sibling branches under that geography, or whether they genuinely need to be separate, independently-evolving territory models, because forcing three real dimensions into one rigid hierarchy usually backfires eventually. Overlapping coverage is something Enterprise Territory Management handles natively — a rep can sit in multiple territories at once — but I wouldn't default every one of those assignments to the same access level. A rep's actual relationship to their primary territory versus one they're just covering for visibility is usually different, so I'd make that an explicit, deliberate role-per-assignment decision, not a default.
