I'd also want to understand how the original estimate was off by 10x in the first place — was it a stale assumption, a misunderstanding between the two systems, a genuine recent change in how much that external system is actually being used — because that's not just about fixing this estimate, that's about fixing how we validate volume assumptions before we ever start building the next integration.
commonMistakes: Quietly tries to work around the discrepancy without surfacing it to stakeholders
Brings the problem to stakeholders without first assessing concrete impact and a revised plan
Frames the discovery as a failure or apologizes excessively instead of framing it as new information
Doesn't investigate the root cause of the 10x estimate miss to improve future requirements-gathering
keyPoints: Surfaces the discovery immediately and transparently rather than quietly absorbing it
Assesses concrete impact and a revised plan before bringing it to stakeholders
Frames the conversation honestly as new information changing the plan, not a failure
Investigates the root cause of the original estimate miss to improve future processes

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Surfaces the discovery immediately and transparently
Assesses concrete impact and builds a revised plan before escalating
Frames the stakeholder conversation constructively, not as a failure
Investigates and addresses the root cause of the estimate miss

questions.title: Leading the Incident Response When a 2GP Package Upgrade Breaks Multiple Orgs
questions.prompt: Your team ships an updated version of an internal 2GP package used across several business unit orgs. Shortly after rollout, two of the five orgs report broken functionality traced to the package update. How do you lead the response?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer prioritizes immediate stabilization over root-cause investigation in the first moments: assessing whether the affected orgs can be safely rolled back to the prior package version (which 2GP unlocked packages generally support via a version downgrade, though this needs to be verified against whether the new version introduced any irreversible data or schema change that would make rollback unsafe), and communicating directly and promptly with the two affected business units about the known impact and the immediate stabilization plan, rather than going quiet while root-cause work happens, since affected business stakeholders experiencing broken functionality need to know what's being done right now, not just eventually what caused it. Once the affected orgs are stabilized (via rollback or a fast-tracked fix, whichever is safe and faster), the investigation should determine why the issue appeared in only two of the five orgs rather than all five, since that's the single most informative fact about root cause — the two affected orgs likely have some meaningful difference (a custom configuration, a dependent package at a different version, a different data state, or usage of a code path the other three orgs don't exercise) that the pre-release validation didn't cover, and finding that specific difference points directly at the gap in the release testing process. The incident review should treat this as a release-process gap rather than purely a code bug: the test coverage or validation scratch orgs used before this release apparently didn't represent the full diversity of configurations across the five actual target orgs, so the durable fix includes expanding pre-release validation to cover that diversity (testing the package against a representative scratch org or sandbox configuration modeled on each business unit's actual customizations, not just a generic clean org) rather than only fixing the specific bug that caused this incident, since the next release could just as easily expose a different gap in the same insufficiently diverse validation process.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is stabilizing the two broken orgs, not investigating why yet — I'd check whether we can safely roll back to the prior package version, which 2GP unlocked packages generally support, as long as the new version didn't make some irreversible data or schema change that would make a rollback unsafe. And I'd be talking directly to those two business units right away about what's broken and what we're doing about it, not going quiet while we dig into root cause — people experiencing broken functionality need to know what's happening right now, not just eventually why it happened. Once those two orgs are stable, the question I actually care about most is why only two of the five orgs broke, not all five or none — that's the most useful fact we have, because it means something's meaningfully different about those two orgs, whether that's a custom configuration, a dependent package at a different version, or some code path only they exercise, and whatever that difference is, it's exactly what our pre-release testing didn't cover. I'd treat this incident review as a release-process gap, not just a code bug — our validation apparently didn't represent the real diversity across all five target orgs, so the actual fix isn't just patching this one bug, it's expanding how we validate future releases to cover that diversity, because otherwise the next release just exposes a different gap in the same insufficiently representative testing.
commonMistakes: Jumps straight to root-cause investigation before stabilizing the affected orgs
Doesn't communicate promptly and directly with the affected business units during the incident
Doesn't investigate why only two of the five orgs were affected, missing the most informative clue
Treats this purely as a code bug fix instead of a release-validation process gap
keyPoints: Prioritizes immediate stabilization (rollback assessment) over root-cause investigation first
Communicates promptly and directly with affected business units during the incident
Investigates why only two of five orgs were affected as the key diagnostic clue
Treats the incident as a release-validation process gap requiring a durable process fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly prioritizes stabilization before root-cause investigation
Communicates promptly and transparently with affected stakeholders
Investigates the correct, most informative diagnostic question
Proposes a durable release-validation process fix, not just a bug patch

questions.title: Reflecting on a Past Architecture Decision That Didn't Scale
questions.prompt: Tell me about an architecture decision you made that didn't hold up as the system scaled, and what you would do differently now.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer gives a specific, real-sounding example with genuine technical detail rather than a vague or deflected non-answer, demonstrating the self-awareness to actually own a decision that didn't hold up rather than attributing the failure entirely to external factors (changing requirements, factors nobody could have predicted) in a way that conveniently absolves the candidate of any responsibility. A credible example should explain the reasoning that seemed sound at the time (the decision wasn't reckless or careless given what was known then — for instance, choosing hand-built sharing rules for a sharing model that was genuinely small and simple at the time, which only became a liability once the object grew into LDV territory years later and nobody revisited the original design assumption), which is a more honest and more useful kind of answer than either 'I was simply wrong' or 'nobody could have known,' since most architecture decisions that age poorly were reasonable given the information and scale available at decision time, and the real lesson is usually about what signal should have triggered revisiting the decision sooner, not that the original decision itself was a mistake. The candidate should articulate a concrete, specific change in practice that resulted from this experience — for example, now explicitly documenting the scale/volume assumptions a given architecture decision is valid under, with a named revisit trigger (e.g., 'revisit sharing model if this object crosses 5 million records') rather than leaving decisions implicitly valid forever until someone happens to notice a problem — demonstrating that the lesson actually changed how the candidate works going forward, not just that they feel appropriately bad about the outcome. The answer should avoid both extremes: neither minimizing the real cost of the decision not scaling (users were affected, remediation took real effort) nor dramatizing it into an exaggerated catastrophe, landing on an honest, specific, proportionate account that a hiring manager can trust reflects genuine experience rather than a rehearsed or fabricated answer.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them about a sharing model I built using straightforward criteria-based sharing rules on an object that, at the time, had maybe a few hundred thousand records and a simple access pattern — it was a completely reasonable call given what I knew then, not a careless one. The problem is that object grew into the tens of millions over the next couple of years, and nobody — including me — ever revisited that original sharing design as it grew, so eventually sharing recalculation started taking hours and causing real user-facing problems whenever the role hierarchy changed. I wasn't wrong given what I knew at the time, but I also don't think 'nobody could have known' is really honest either — the real gap was that I never documented the scale assumption that design was actually valid under, so there was no trigger telling anyone, including future me, to come back and reconsider it as the object grew. What actually changed in how I work because of that: I now explicitly write down the volume and scale assumptions any architecture decision is valid under, with a specific number that should trigger revisiting it — something like 'revisit this sharing model if this object crosses five million records' — instead of leaving a decision implicitly valid forever until someone happens to notice it's become a problem.
commonMistakes: Gives a vague, deflected, or fabricated-sounding non-answer instead of a specific real example
Blames the failure entirely on unpredictable external factors, avoiding any real ownership
Overcorrects into 'I was simply wrong' without explaining why the decision was reasonable at the time
Doesn't articulate a concrete, specific change in practice resulting from the experience
keyPoints: Gives a specific, credible example with genuine technical detail
Honestly explains why the decision was reasonable given information available at the time
Identifies what signal should have triggered revisiting the decision sooner
Describes a concrete, specific change in practice resulting from the experience

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a specific, credible, technically detailed example
Honestly explains the reasoning at the time without deflecting blame
Identifies the correct lesson (revisit trigger) rather than just 'I was wrong'
Describes a concrete, lasting change in practice
